criticReviews.excerpt: Jason Manford is a charming, showtune-obsessed homicide cop in this fun companion to Chicago and Cabaret.

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: If anything, this breathtakingly thrilling production by Jamie Lloyd - and the tour-de-force central performance by James McAvoy as the eponymous, big-nosed soldier-poet - have only become deeper and richer since the 2019 premiere. Maybe the last two years have made its themes of separation and loss more profound.

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: It’s a daringly contemporary re-working which will be remembered for one of the most imposing performances of the decade. [However] the slackening of pace in the second half was unmistakable.

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: Don’t mention the nose. That’s the warning offered to anyone in the vicinity of Cyrano de Bergerac, who, in James McAvoy’s fiercely charismatic portrayal, is a powder keg of a man: one quip about his legendarily large proboscis and he’s apt to explode.

criticReviews.author: Caroline McGinn
criticReviews.excerpt: Writers are fighters and the word is everything in this firecracker show about passion, rejection, and the crazy genius of the spoken word. The rapiers, intrigue and censorship of Cardinal Richelieu’s Paris, circa 1640, are modernised as razor-sharp banter about love, sex, and – nudge, wink – cultural appropriation.

criticReviews.author: Natasha Tripney
criticReviews.excerpt: Lloyd’s production delights in the music of voices – coupled with the Ringham brothers’ sound design and Vaneeka Dadhria’s beatboxing – it continually underscores the fact that this play is, as much as anything, an impassioned love letter to the power of words.

criticReviews.author: Mark Shenton
criticReviews.excerpt: I wouldn't necessarily want all my classics to be delivered in this way, but Lloyd's company is committed to attracting a youthful audience...

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: Complex ideas about love, literature, body image and truth are expressed in its dizzyingly clever rhymes, but essentially it remains a captivating, tragicomic romance.

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: It doesn’t have the euphoric effortlessness and virtuoso authenticity of ‘Hamilton’; but it’s not a million miles off...Lloyd and co have cooked up something pretty remarkable.

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: I’ve barely scratched the surface of a show that cuts to the core of a classic and what it means to be alive. I defy anyone not to fall in love with it.

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: But once you accept that Lloyd has jettisoned much of the period detail for a reason, you can concentrate on the play’s psychological complexities. There is nothing fey or decorative.

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: It is a triumph, a breathtakingly bold rethinking of a classic in resonant contemporary ways.

criticReviews.author: Aleks Sierz
criticReviews.excerpt: You leave the theatre enriched by the superb wit of the writing, the energy and sincerity of the performances and the supreme theatrical imagination that has put all this together. I dare you to miss it.

criticReviews.author: Michael Billington
criticReviews.excerpt: But I found myself gradually warming to this radical deconstruction of Rostand’s heroic comedy and totally captivated by James McAvoy’s performance as the swaggering Gascon.

criticReviews.author: Paul Taylor
criticReviews.excerpt: This new season looks set for the kind of success Lloyd and company had last year with their marvellous Pinter retrospective. Bravo.

criticReviews.author: Natasha Tripney
criticReviews.excerpt: James mcavoy radiates charisma...Yes there are times when Lloyd’s production feels like it’s striving too hard to generate a hip, post-Hamilton vibe, but it tempers this with a sense of humour.

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The way the book merrily hopscotches from cliché to cliché can still raise smiles. But 'Dames' ultimately founders on our familiarity, not with the genre it plays with like a cat’s toy, but with the long history, since its creation, of similar simulations of old-school entertainments. Even housed in Broadway’s smallest theater, this miniature musical, with a cast you could fit in a dinghy, seems just a little, well, at sea."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "It lands like a harmless piece of wet fluff. The first 20 minutes of wide-eyed antics are cute; then your mind starts to wander. 'Dames at Sea's' mild pastiche is passable but passé—imagine a revival, half a century from now, of a Fringe show about the ’80s—and it’s presented with tongue so far in cheek that it can’t say much at all."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Instead of sticking close to the presentational style of Busby Berkeley spectaculars, 'Dames' literally belittled itself, making do with a cast of six and an orchestra of three on a stage barely big enough to contain Bernadette Peters. It would seem to be a category error to bring material so conceived to Broadway, and the production that just opened at the Helen Hayes, much as you root for it, fails to argue otherwise."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "What’s not to like? Nothing whatsoever—but there isn’t enough to love about 'Dames at Sea,' which may have seemed sufficiently witty a half-century ago but has long since been outclassed by the encyclopedically knowing musical-comedy spoofery of 'The Drowsy Chaperone.' Compared with that big-brain homage, 'Dames' isn’t much more clever than a college show, and its parodies steer too close to their models to be other than mildly amusing."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "‘Dames At Sea’ is a lot of fun and a tribute to the city’s inexhaustible pool of inexhaustible talent, if not actual stars…Broadway today is awash in nostalgia in the form of revivals, reboots and parodies, all done on a far larger scale and offering considerably more bang, or tap, for the buck. And good as they are, the dancers never let us forget just how hard they’re working to please us."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Dames at Sea' is a mid-1960s musical trifle that works overtime to be cheeky good fun. Thanks to a cast with twinkle-toes and polished pipes, it succeeds — for a while. Before long, though, monotony sets in and won’t go away. Even top-notch tap-dancing can get repetitive...'Dames' doesn’t make a big splash or sink. It treads water."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "The new leading lady of 'Dames at Sea' is no Bernadette Peters. There’s nothing wrong with this revival that Peters, who played the role of Ruby in the original, couldn’t fix. But musical theater stars of her caliber don’t grow on trees, and although newcomer Eloise Kropp is a power tapper par excellence, she hasn’t the saucy charm of a Broadway Baby like Ruby — or the magnetic appeal of a star like Peters."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Dames at Sea' reinvents one of those big-screen spectacles as a shrunken stage musical — a baby Busby Berkeley if you will — with an appealing cast of six that makes its featherweight pleasures infectious...A sweet candy morsel serving unapologetically empty calories."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "NYTimes Critic's Pick!...“Dana H.” is not just the story of a woman brutalized by a psychopath; it is also the story of a mother abandoned by a son. What else would a playwright do to make reparations but write a play about just that, in the process returning to her what the world had stolen: her voice."

criticReviews.author: Juan Michael Porter II
criticReviews.excerpt: "I recently reviewed a show and declared that talk business does not belong onstage. Dana H. has forced me to eat my words and to accept that there are no absolutes in theatre, particularly when the story is horrifically affecting and spectacularly executed as this show is. Dana H. should be required viewing for legal scholars, law enforcement officers, and aspirants across the country, if only to remind them that depravity reigns when they fail to do the right thing."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Five stars!...O’Connell is nothing less than astonishing...Watching Dana H. is like listening to a fascinating true-crime podcast, and part of the interest is in the mysteries that adhere to Dana’s account, which may be distorted by trauma and time."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mr. Waters has staged it with the utmost simplicity, trusting in the force of the tale. I have never watched a more powerful piece of documentary theater: Once seen, it will stay with you for a long time to come."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "A mesmerizing act of electronic ventriloquism...It’s hard to say which is more absorbing: Dana’s story or O’Connell’s uncanny portrayal, requiring her to reproduce in perfect alignment with the audiotape every cough, pause, giggle and slap of the chair in which she sits for much of the 75 minutes of the piece."

criticReviews.author: Matt Windman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Given the lip-synching and lack of movement on the part of O’Connell, one may wonder why “Dana H.” needs to be a live piece of theater rather than a true crime podcast or a raw testimonial video on YouTube. But at its best, the production (directed by Les Waters, who has also staged other plays by Hnath) is compelling, terrifying, and multilayered, especially with regard to the nature of reality."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "Not only is it the wildest true story on any stage in New York City, but it features a performance that must be seen to be believed."

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: "A theatre piece that unmistakably demands considerable thought and even more unmistakably boasts Deirdre O’Connell’s unbounded talents."

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: " As enchanting as this setting is, it’s also ruled by pitiless patriarchal Catholicism. "

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Even if you missed all the subtext, this show would still delight in its acute depiction of family dynamics...This play won Friel the Evening Standard Award for best play in 1991, and it still looks richly deserved."

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Movement lies at the emotional heart of this play and it is orchestrated with such delicate mastery by Wayne McGregor that the stomping scene, featuring the sisters dancing with wild abandon is a shared hedonistic escape, rebellious ritual and act of worship in one."

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: "The crux of ‘Dancing at Lughnasa’ is that it’s a sort of happy tragedy...It’s not bliss, but it is community, safety, sisterhood warmth, and dancing. A beautiful production of a beautiful play."

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "The scale of the Olivier – transformed into a bucolic paradise that seems to stretch as far as Tipperary – can work against the work’s subtlety and nuance, audibility an occasional issue."

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: "The poetry seldom takes flight. Mark Henderson’s subtle lighting lends depth, though, to a production that gives the past a shimmering golden halo."

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: "The judgement of each performance makes this portrait of a family deeply affecting, but every aspect of the production honours a play that feels as fresh as the day it was written."

criticReviews.author: Matt Wolf
criticReviews.excerpt: “This production may throw different aspects of the play into bold relief...but the play's sense of ectasy dampened down by circumstance, and worse, allows its putative intimacy to fill the reaches of the Olivier”

criticReviews.author: Sam Marlowe
criticReviews.excerpt: "It is a production of piercing lyricism as well as embracing warmth and wit: gorgeous."

criticReviews.author: Daz Gale
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Dancing at Lughnasa’ is a show that might take its time to grab your interest, but when it does it will have you hooked. Utterly captivating and at times unconventional in its approach, its refreshingly different storytelling device, impressive set design and truly outstanding cast ensure this is an overall winning show”

criticReviews.author: Isobel Lewis
criticReviews.excerpt: “When Michael looks back at his life, it’s the women he remembers – and in Rourke’s production, they’re what we remember too. The women and the dancing.”

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: "Haddad - he will change the way you think about disability — and prompt you to think of accessibility as something that can deepen a dramatic experience when it’s built into the architecture of the piece."

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine
criticReviews.excerpt: “Jordan Fein’s skillful direction balances the laughter with a well-paced dosing of the grim truth — New York City, like the world, is not built for disabled people. Media often represents the disabled experience as monolithic, but ‘Dark Disabled Stories’ includes a variety of lenses.”

criticReviews.author: Melissa Rose Bernardo
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show does feel a bit short. Is it greedy to want a few more vignettes to let us spend more time with these dynamic performers? Here’s hoping these Stories are just Haddad’s first volume."

criticReviews.author: Christian Lewis
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Dark Disabled Stories' offers a model of how to do theater better, in ways that are more accommodating, accessible, and accepting of all people and bodies."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “You can check any sentimental notions at the door of this eye-opening, often hilarious, and sometimes scathing exercise…This collection of first-person accounts features surtitles, sign language by the Deaf actor Dickie Hearts, and audio description by Alejandra Ospina, who uses a wheelchair. Although most of Dark Disabled Stories is devoted to Haddad's pitiless stories of navigating the indifferent world of the abled, his co-stars weigh in, too, on everything from taking the subway to picking up a sexual partner; as they make blazingly clear, even the simplest activity can require considerable guts and nerve.”

criticReviews.author: Wendy Caster
criticReviews.excerpt: "Most of 'Dark Disabled Stories' ultimately centers on people not listening and not recognizing each other's humanity. The show depicts this vividly in a worthwhile 75 minutes in the theatre."

criticReviews.author: Sandy MacDonald
criticReviews.excerpt: “Haddad does have a gift for finding the light – the humor – lurking in the ‘dark.’”

criticReviews.author: David Walters
criticReviews.excerpt: “The play is a compilation of humorous and honest stories about constantly confronting an obstacle, both physical and emotional, in a world not built to accommodate who you are.”

criticReviews.author: Loren Noveck
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show is also an investigation into modes of theatrical communication; at times it feels like a thought experiment as much as a theater piece."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: the most accessible play I’ve ever attended; it even expands the concept of accessible, and certainly drives it home. Much of the show is also hilarious. Some of the stories are raunchy or foul-mouthed; some are suspenseful; some make us feel exasperated along with Ryan. "Dark Disabled Stories" is rarely dark. It is always entertaining, and eye-opening.

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Dark Disabled Stories’ is a show about forging connections, including intimate ones, and building empathy for those who experience the world differently and meeting them on their own terms.”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "...it is too cluttered — stylistically, tonally, ideologically — to offer much insight."

criticReviews.author: Austin Fimmano
criticReviews.excerpt: "Because 'Dark Noon' is a depiction of the Wild West, there is a lot of onstage violence"

criticReviews.author: Raven Snook
criticReviews.excerpt: "4/5 Stars! The Wild West looms large in American self-mythology."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "...'Dark Noon' becomes, for a few minutes at least, sharply personal and compelling."

criticReviews.author: Kenji Fujishima
criticReviews.excerpt: "is a funhouse-mirror retelling of American history: specifically, the 19th-century era"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “The play views history through so many filters that the result is blurred.”

criticReviews.author: Stanford Friedman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dark Noon sheds light on often overlooked facts"

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "...such a rollicking entertainment"

criticReviews.author: Mark Rifkin
criticReviews.excerpt: "The lawless of the wild West"

criticReviews.author: Edward Karam
criticReviews.excerpt: Dark Noon is an energetic juggernaut, but one wishes the show had a more discerning eye.

criticReviews.author: Tim Teeman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Right now, 'Data' feels all-too present, all-too raw and indisputably somber"

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine
criticReviews.excerpt: “This moral-dilemma play contains several unexpected twists and turns, including a few that draw audible gasps from the audience.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s a correct if obvious idea, here rendered as didactically as if we’re watching a medieval morality play.”

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "Data is essential viewing for anyone who wants to understand the dystopia the AI revolution is leading to, and why it is succeeding"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "The debuting playwright Matthew Libby invents an all-too-plausible scenario in which the future of American democracy hangs on an algorithm's performance, putting the outcome in the hands of a callow, troubled recent college graduate. Scary enough for you?

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: “With Data, Michael Libby has written an unquestionably significant play wrenched not only from today’s headlines but possibly also ripped from headlines heading our way in the frightfully near future.”

criticReviews.author: Roma Torre
criticReviews.excerpt: "Data is a serious play but there is humor, almost exclusively in the hands of Jonah who knows his limitations but compensates by taking on the persona of an over-stimulated dude. "

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: Techno-thriller that is taken from tomorrow's headlines is one scary trip and very provocative about ICE's next step.

criticReviews.author: James Wilson
criticReviews.excerpt: "David is undeniably worth rooting for"

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: reduces the life of its hero to a series of political events, but it entertains throughout

criticReviews.author: Marc Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: Tapper, who composed the music unassisted, aims for an old-timey melodic sound.

criticReviews.author: Paulanne Simmons
criticReviews.excerpt: "Impressive performances and a formidable score"

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: "Gone is the emotional aridity that kept the story at a strange remove."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Kelli O'Hara and Brian d'Arcy James give career-best performances"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "If 'Days and Wine and Roses' isn’t exactly galvanizing...it is effectively sober."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "...the show evokes a specific kind of quietly disheartened sigh."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show...has a searing power that leaves you both stirred and shaken."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "despite its somber theme, Days of Wine and Roses is sumptuous from start to finish"

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: " ‘Days of Wine and Roses,’ a ‘beautifully’ executed musical"

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: "There are plenty of joys and sorrows to play even in a straightforward cautionary tale."

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: "If not for the unbridled drinking, it might easily have been a screwball comedy...Directed in its world premiere by Michael Greif for Atlantic Theater Company, this 'Days of Wine and Roses' fills the old Gothic Revival parish house that is the Linda Gross Theater with glorious sound."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Despite some moving moments, 'Days of Wine and Roses' is a downbeat musical cocktail that doesn’t expand or enhance the source material."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "Kirsten and Joe’s dissolution, though telegraphed and executed with precision, is more abstract than gutting. You can see the rails of the plot too clearly, one character trading positions with another, and that distracts from seeing them fully as a people and from a more complex understanding of the disease. The approach is decorous."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: “The thorns pierce deeply in the new musical ‘Days of Wine and Roses.’ And not just for the main characters, a loving couple who see their marriage, and their lives, spiraling out of control in the throttling grip of alcoholism.”

criticReviews.author: Rex Reed
criticReviews.excerpt: "As a ruthless account of the fate that wrecks the lives of decent people, this is a grim, graphic, and demanding play, but as a musical, I watched them suffer but just wasn’t able to suffer with them the same way. In 'The Days of Wine and Roses,' there’s plenty of wine, but you won’t go away humming any roses."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Days of Wine and Roses' returns us to the middle of the last century, when alcoholism was perhaps more of a hot-button social issue. But its catalyzing role in a co-dependent relationship remains dramatically interesting"

criticReviews.author: David Gordon
criticReviews.excerpt: "If you’re looking for the feel-bad hit of the summer, the Atlantic has you covered...'Days of Wine and Roses' might be a harrowing watch, but you’ll never see anything like it again."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “They've watered down the wine in this well-intentioned but strangely stilted musical about the ravages of boozing. Blake Edwards' 1962 film, written by JP Miller…remains an astonishingly frank and ugly account of a marriage destroyed by alcoholism, not least for the unsparing performances of Jack Lemmon and Lee Remick. As sometimes happens, however, the process of transforming such sharp-edged material into musical theatre hasn't added anything new or essential. Seeing it the other day at the Atlantic, I kept wondering why anyone thought Days of Wine and Roses needed to be a musical at all.”

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "With such a sad and tragic tale, what we miss is a much-needed depth in the unfolding of the plot. Things do seem to lose their way toward the end...Above all, and despite the show's flaws, the score and James and O'Hara's singing guarantee a most memorable evening."

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: "This 'Days of Wine and Roses' is a musical, though the term “musical” may be slightly misleading...This 100-minute, intermissionless piece — which clearly regards the traditional, 20th century, 32-bar song as a thing of the far distant past — is more of an opera and calls for putting aside any questions about its suitability for being musicalized, since it unflinchingly depicts dire situations."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s obvious that 'Days of Wine and Roses' is a deeply felt effort — Guettel has made no secret of his own addiction issues in his past — and the piece has much to recommend it. But one ultimately comes away feeling more admiring than shattered."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: Lucas’ script remains faithful to Miller’s teleplay (with the excision of Joe’s delirium tremens in the psycho ward or his second hospitalization) and much of the dialogue is actually Miller’s. However, the problem is the score. Guettel’s 18 songs (including four reprises) are often atonal, unmelodic, unrhymed and don’t scan. While this is true of the Tony Award-winning "The Light in the Piazza" that score had such a lush sound that it was automatically romantic and appropriate for its story. Here it is almost as though Guettel is striving for opera but without the orchestral underpinnings to make it so.

criticReviews.author: Carol Rocamora
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s no small accomplishment that a musical with a topic as serious as ‘Days of Wine and Roses’ can provide catharsis and, at the same time, offer the hope of redemption.”

criticReviews.author: Tulis McCall
criticReviews.excerpt: "To be certain, this is an odd choice for a musical.  The writers take on a dangerous topic – and that is brave.  I think they wanted to show us the underbelly of this beast of alcoholism and its ability to overwhelm the most well-intentioned among us.  This show succeeds in doing so."

criticReviews.author: Erin Kahn
criticReviews.excerpt: "While it works well as a cautionary tale about the dangers of addiction and the epidemic of alcoholism in America, 'Days of Wine and Roses' isn't quite as effective as a piece of musical theatre...Despite its failings, it's a chillingly powerful illustration of how completely addiction can ruin a person and a family, and, as always, O'Hara dazzles."

criticReviews.author: Elyse Trevers
criticReviews.excerpt: “Generally, I would encourage everyone to rush out to buy a ticket to anything O’ Hara appears in. With her wholesome presence, blonde beauty and crystal- clear soprano voice, she adds class and talent to every show. Unfortunately this musical doesn’t do her justice.”

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: The breathtaking performances by Brian d’Arcy James and Kelli O’Hara are enough justification for this stage adaptation of the sad, dark story about a couple who fall in love with alcohol. But there is also a brilliance that suffuses Adam Guettel’s score, and periodically poke out in Craig Lucas’s book, that make any shortcomings I might see in the show feel irrelevant.

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: "And full truth be told, you’ll leave this unusual show 105 minutes later without a truly satisfactory answer, yet unbearably grateful to have heard the clarion, celestial voices of the wonderful Kelli O’Hara and Brian D’Arcy James...as well as the often-gorgeous melodies created by the prodigiously talented Adam Guettel."

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: Guettel’s lyrics, which focus attention on the intense interactions of Joe and Kirsten, could not be more potently rendered than by Brian d’Arcy James and Kelli O’Hara, two of New York’s foremost stage presences. Under Michael Greif’s sensitive direction...their good looks, stunning acting skills, and dazzling voices of extraordinary range and power make Days of Wine and Roses worth a visit, even if it means swallowing the downer of a script.

criticReviews.author: Robert Hofler
criticReviews.excerpt: "As with so many musicals derived from movies rather than plays, “Days of Wine and Roses” is chockfull of scenes...Perhaps on a large stage with more physical resources, some of these directorial longueurs can be reduced or eliminated."

criticReviews.author: James Wilson
criticReviews.excerpt: “The cumulative effects are impressive, but in the end, ‘Days of Wine and Roses’ is more intellectually stimulating than intoxicatingly soul-stirring.”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Dead Outlaw,' the feel-good musical of the season, if death and deadpan feel good to you."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: “Dead Outlaw...is entertainment for a paying audience, after all.”

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "That same level of commitment extends to all of Dead Outlaw. The writing is piquant and sly, the songs have verve and resonance, and every element of Cromer’s production seems to fit exactly in place."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dead Outlaw’s peculiarities are enhanced by the way it foregrounds its cast’s own idiosyncrasies."

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: "The musical has many diamonds in the rough. They’re just not polished properly by Cromer’s staging, which is awfully haphazard and diffuse for a typically sure-thing director."

criticReviews.author: Emlyn Travis
criticReviews.excerpt: "The pair are singing a much different, more raucous tune as they transform Elmer's larger-than-life story into a rollicking, country rock concert complete with a whole lot of laughs and a surprising amount of heart."

criticReviews.author: Joseph Verlezza
criticReviews.excerpt: “Andrew Durand as Elmer McCurdy has certainly turned “playing dead” into an artform.”

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: ‘Dead Outlaw’ unearths the corpse of forgotten history to an infectious rockabilly beat — elevating a twisty little yarn into a bizarro-world elegy to how the American Dream can curdle into violence, cruelty, and casual indifference.

criticReviews.author: Laura Collins-Hughes
criticReviews.excerpt: "...a compact, deliciously deadpan yarn that stretches over almost a century."

criticReviews.author: Amelia Merrill
criticReviews.excerpt: "new musical tells a larger-than-life-and-death true story"

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "With wit and vigor, Dead Outlaw investigates a country obsessed with liberty and heroism"

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s a doozy of a debut and a sharp departure from the writers’ last show."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “…a mildly tedious exercise that beats a single idea into oblivion”

criticReviews.author: James Wilson
criticReviews.excerpt: "...the show is a fantastic and biting satire on American greed and capitalism"

criticReviews.author: Joseph Pisano
criticReviews.excerpt: "visually unruly and dramatically inert"

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: Despite its title, there’s nothing dead about this lively musical.

criticReviews.author: Tulis McCall
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Dead Outlaw' is not so much a musical as it is a play with music."

criticReviews.author: Joseph Verlezza
criticReviews.excerpt: “Mr. Yazbek turns in a score that is extremely varied including rockabilly, pop rock"

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: self-conscious slice of Americana almost as creepy as clever,less resonant than it intends

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: "it’s very satisfying while it goes down, but only leaves you full for a couple of hours."

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Dead Outlaw' unearths the corpse of forgotten history"

criticReviews.author: Mark Rifkin
criticReviews.excerpt: "As dysfunctional as the first part of Elmer McCurdy's life was"

criticReviews.author: Deirdre Donovan
criticReviews.excerpt: Dead Outlaw tells the true story of an outlaw who gained fame after his death.

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "...it is full of little surprises, inside jokes, catty repartee...campy performances"

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: "an attempt to outdo Charles Busch’s output without having the wit to bring it off"

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: Deadly Stages is all that its title promises.

criticReviews.author: Darryl Reilly
criticReviews.excerpt: "An aging Broadway diva is gloriously performed by a man in drag"

criticReviews.author: Edward Karam
criticReviews.excerpt: "The plot itself leans heavily into melodrama."

criticReviews.author: Julia Rank
criticReviews.excerpt: “James Graham’s multi-faceted play ‘Dear England,’ in Rupert Goold’s tremendous production, has the sweep and crowd-pleasing energy of a musical; it’s both populist and deeply thoughtful, and told with such warmth and wit that football fanatics and sceptics alike will probably be willing to die for Southgate and his team by the end.”

criticReviews.author: Daz Gale
criticReviews.excerpt: “While the acting and direction are as good as it gets, it really is the writing that puts Dear England at the top of the league...The way this play manages to connect with its audience, finding its way into their very soul, is something few shows manage to achieve successfully. “

criticReviews.author: Greg Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: “When the curtain falls it’s a case of ‘they think it’s all over’ but of course this time, it’s not. Outside a West End theatre, Southgate remains in the job and shows no signs of going anytime soon. So, although Graham doesn’t have a true ending to this story, Dear England stands proud as a joyful portrayal of the game, and a heartfelt celebration of teamwork.”

criticReviews.author: Dominic Maxwell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Rupert Goold, never one to leave his showmanship in the locker room, has rarely married storytelling with spectacle with more of a flourish. Between him and Graham and an ensemble so good it would be invidious to pick out individuals (sorry, lads) they ensure that a huge cast of characters are delineated with wit and clarity."

criticReviews.author: Claire Allfree
criticReviews.excerpt: “Against a fracturing sense of national identity, ‘’Dear England’ makes manifest the everyday glue that binds us...God knows what the tourists will make of it. No matter. This is a rare and special thing – a play that dares to let us feel not so bad about being us.”

criticReviews.author: Helen Hawkins
criticReviews.excerpt: “This is still a terrific evening of navel-gazing that the nation has to keep doing, in search of an answer to what it means in these post-Brexit days to be not just an England footballer, but English.”

criticReviews.author: Mary Pollard
criticReviews.excerpt: “James Graham’s superb play ‘Dear England’ is a love letter not only to the sport, but to the power it has to affect change across a nation and within individuals. An extraordinarily inspiring and enlightening production, it explores human possibility and positive transformation through football, demonstrating how beautiful relationships can be generated when care is taken.”

criticReviews.author: George Rennie
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Dear England’ is a play for our conflicted and troubled country, exploring the complexities of fandom and national pride in such a joyful way, whilst allowing space to recognise the racism...it’s a beautifully clear, rousing, and celebratory exploration of football that has the power to reach the hearts of even the most uninitiated audience members, and give them the chance to feel it all, from the inside out.”

criticReviews.author: Callum Wallace
criticReviews.excerpt: “It is Rupert Goold’s direction that maintains the play’s momentum. There is never a dull moment here as we move through scenes with the finely tuned detail of a football player dribbling across the pitch, darting this way and that but always with one goal in mind...This performance is truly universal and speaks to something greater than the sum of its parts.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The marvelous young actor Ben Platt is giving a performance that’s not likely to be bettered on Broadway this season. What’s more, this gorgeous heartbreaker of a musical has grown in emotional potency during its journey to the big leagues...The musical finds endless nuances in the relationships among its characters...Under the superb direction of the veteran Michael Greif, the show has been subtly refined, its brasher comedy softened, and the performances have grown in delicacy."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Platt is giving one of the greatest leading male performances I’ve ever seen in a musical, and the thrillingly modern and moving 'Dear Evan Hansen' is worthy of it...The musical benefits mightily from Greif’s dynamic direction, Korins’s vivid set design, Nigrini's cascading projections and an excellent cast...Benj Pasek and Justin Paul’s score brims with tuneful and thoughtful songs...And Levenson’s book is unfailingly smart...'Dear Evan Hansen' must be seen to be believed."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "So fine in its craft and rich in its gathering of themes that it rewards being seen again—and again...Platt imbues the character with so much pathos and lively detail that he succeeds as the story’s engine despite being almost pathologically passive...That Levenson has been able to find spots for humor at all in this grippingly sad story, and that Pasek and Paul have been able to turn those opportunities into songs of comic relief is a sign of the size of the ideas in play."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s smartly crafted, emotionally open-hearted and ideally cast. What’s more, it’s pitched to and has been embraced by millennials...yet its appeal is universal...Michael Greif has staged 'Dear Evan Hansen' with fluid, fast-moving simplicity...The score is not quite as strong as Steven Levenson’s ingenious book...Still, the songs work on their own terms, and the book is strong enough that it could be done on its own as a play...The best musical to open on Broadway since 'Hamilton.'"

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "The score by Pasek and Paul is packed with engaging tunes and insightful lyrics. The book by Levenson portrays teen angst taken beyond the normal boundaries with compelling dignity...Platt plays the title role in a movingly sensitive, career-making performance...Platt seems more to inhabit Evan than to merely portray him...The score soars, bringing us along with it. 'Dear Evan Hansen' is an intimate show with a gigantic heart."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Platt nails each shifting mood and tone as a socially inept outcast. Original and up-to-the-minute, the musical has a lot to say—about parents and children, social media, and more...Stirring ballads and rousing group songs in the vibrant, varied score by Benj Pasek and Justin Paul ooze emotions. Director Michael Greif excels at guiding actors through complex stories—and his work has never been better...The show's so satisfying it deserves a thank-you note."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "Not since 'Next to Normal' has a score tapped so deeply into the troubled psyche of its needy protagonist...The lyrics go beyond the spoken thought and reach for the unspoken feelings hiding behind the words. Better yet, there’s not a hint of sentimentality...Under the thoughtful direction of Greif, Platt goes beyond physical specificity to get under Evan’s skin and into his unsettled mind.  And the introspective, gentle score becomes the language of his troubled thoughts and yearnings."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "What's perhaps most distinctive about Pasek and Paul's melodic emo-pop score is how beautifully it captures the peaks and valleys of adolescence, in the thoughtful lyrics and in the music itself...Playwright Steven Levenson matches the musical components beat for beat in his terrific book, which sets up with persuasive conviction what could easily have been a contrived premise...Across the board, the ensemble is superb, each of them registering rich moments of emotional complexity."

criticReviews.author: Mark Shenton
criticReviews.excerpt: Benj Pasek and Justin Paul's beautiful score may be a little ballad-heavy, but has integrity and depth that matches the story they have to tell, whose book is written by Steven Levenson.

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: [The production] looks odd and overdone in London. Ultimately, this is a high school drama about stalkers, trolls and those who piggyback on tragedy. Which may be a tough sell for a London musical audience.

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: Directed (as on Broadway) by Michael Greif, the evening has - all the same - no weak links, casting-wise. But the show belongs to its 21-year-old star Sam Tutty, fresh out of drama school and making his West End debut.

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: Yet if the prospect of spending an evening contemplating the perils of peer pressure, family breakdown and rampant social media seems less than inviting, be reassured that Dear Evan Hansen is worth it.

criticReviews.author: Alice Saville
criticReviews.excerpt: A West End newcomer, 21-year-old Sam Tutty glows with sweat and goodness, bringing integrity to a storyline that’s somewhere between ingenious and tortuous.

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: A pat sentiment, perhaps, but worth sharing – and if this modern fable speaks loudest to a new generation of theatregoers, then it’s one we can all cheer.

criticReviews.author: Tim Bano
criticReviews.excerpt: As shown in The Greatest Showman, Pasek and Paul have cracked the formula for four-chord pop songs; songs with a golden touch...Yes, a couple of those in second act are mawkish, but the rest are superb.

criticReviews.author: Alex Wood
criticReviews.excerpt: Dear Evan Hansen is a desperately powerful exploration of a troubled teen sacrificing the truth for a sense of comfort – startlingly relevant for a world swaddled in screens and fleeting fictions.

criticReviews.author: Michael Billington
criticReviews.excerpt: Everything, in fact, is expertly done but, if I didn’t totally surrender to the show, it is because it lacks the courage to admit that high anxiety is not so easily cured.

criticReviews.author: Paul Taylor
criticReviews.excerpt: Sam Tutty gives a star-making performance in a story of grief, deception and the conscienceless juggernaut of the internet.

criticReviews.author: Julia Rank
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dodie Smith's properly laugh-out-loud funny play deserves a further life"

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "This gently witty revival of Dodie Smith’s play rarely provokes more than a wry smile"

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Death...form constant motifs but Smith’s gift for comedy keeps us from the abyss."

criticReviews.author: Dave Fargnoli
criticReviews.excerpt: “Particularly poignant revival of Dodie Smith's comedy”

criticReviews.author: Matt Wolf
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dodie Smith's leisurely play emerges as a real pleasure"

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dodie Smith’s prophetic play mourns a way of life that is already gone"

criticReviews.author: Tim Bano
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dodie Smith’s slow burning pre-war family saga will suck you in"

criticReviews.author: Kate Wyver
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show glides seamlessly."

criticReviews.author: Lucinda Everett
criticReviews.excerpt: "Unpacking all of this is quite the balancing act...Burns’s...manages it beautifully."

criticReviews.author: Caroline McGinn
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s a period curiosity, basically. But this is a pleasant revival."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: “The chance to see two theatrical masterminds go at it for a few hours is sufficient justification for the effort.”

criticReviews.author: Austin Fimmano
criticReviews.excerpt: "There is love and fandom in every element of this show, like recreations of the movie's outfits and iconic lines"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “Having popped its cork early, the show keeps the bubbles flowing freely for the next two hours.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “...hard to dislike and ultimately—as a medical examiner might say of these women—without a heartbeat.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "Megan Hilty and Jennifer Simard give boisterously funny performances as preening rivals"

criticReviews.author: Frank Rizzo
criticReviews.excerpt: “The storyline is cleaner, the characters are clearer, and the pace and the laughs are now non-stop.”

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: “Even if the musical doesn’t have a discernible heartbeat, Hilty and Simard ensure Death Becomes Her stays fun and fabulous.”

criticReviews.author: Dalton Ross
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s a mission that succeeds more often than not.”

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "Having introduced the most unappealing topic in the world, Death, Let Me Do My Show manages to be both harrowing and hilarious; like the best comedy, it is rooted in concerns that are deeply personal yet also hits a universal nerve."

criticReviews.author: Joel Benjamin
criticReviews.excerpt: Dressed in a glittery, silver suit—costumes by Kristin Isola—Bloom immediately takes control of an audience who already admire her from her standup comedy and her bitterly funny TV show, "Crazy Ex-Girlfriend" plus her solo tour of "What Am I Going to Do with My Life Now?" and, perhaps, from the recent iteration of this amusing musing of life and death and birth and Covid. Bloom ponders her pre-pandemic self and the trauma of the birth of her daughter who had a life-threatening condition.  Covid limited her visits to her baby in the NICU and caused the death of her close friend and writing partner Adam Schlesinger who, ironically, shared the NICU when it was partly converted to a Covid ward.

criticReviews.author: Tulis McCall
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Rachel Bloom: Death, Let Me Do My Show’ is an acquired taste. This means you have to keep up with her rapid delivery that lasts a mere 80 minutes. I was not familiar with Ms. Bloom, and I was definitely in the minority – but this did not stop me from keeping up because Bloom is a very articulate and precise performer. She knows exactly where she is going and will do everything she can to make sure you stay on the path.”

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: a show about death, Bloom’s personal experience and personal take on it. But in many ways, the show is also still the glitzy musical standup she initially intended…The result  is certainly clever, undeniably entertaining at times, but also largely hollow. By framing her experiences through a synthetic comic filter, she keeps us at a distance from much of anything meaningful or memorable about this greatest mystery of human existence, or the reactions it inspires – which is to say, fear, grief, cosmic questioning.

criticReviews.author: Colin Macdonald
criticReviews.excerpt: “The songs are wonderfully absurd yet incisive riffs on the ways people grapple with anxiety about death. The show is a comic triumph but stops short of profundity or catharsis, as Bloom seems reluctant to really confront the melancholy inherent in the material...Bloom offers a peak at the darkness that lurks behind the silliness but is sure to keep it at bay and to foreground laughter.”

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: “The songs are the highlights here. Bloom is especially good at puncturing emotion with surreal detail...More than blunt language — a tool that loses its sharpness with use — this absurdist vein effectively draws laughs, but it also underscores the show’s real subject: the often cruel arbitrariness of life.”

criticReviews.author: Amelia Merrill
criticReviews.excerpt: “The show instead leaves the impression that Bloom is rushing to process grief, joy, and the last decade of her career before the pop culture moment moves on. Perhaps with more room for reflection, her next show will strike a different chord.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “Bloom is so good in her default mode, with a glint in her eye and dozens of curse words in her mouth, that she wins you over to her helter-skelter view of the world. She wins Death himself over too, or at least manages to get him to sing along with her about the cum trees.”

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Death’ is a hard sell in 2023, when so many of our feelings about the pandemic remain raw and unprocessed, stowed away in an emotional cupboard so that we can get on with the business of living. But if we must revisit Covid (and eventually, we must) I can think of few more delightful, hilariously tuneful ways.”

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: “Bloom knows her audience and plays to it...Maybe it is occasionally humorous, but it’s got nothing to do with wit. Whereas Bloom gives the ready impression of having the wherewithal for being impressively witty on the challenging subject, death.”

criticReviews.author: Sandy MacDonald
criticReviews.excerpt: “With signature panache and zero regard for propriety, Bloom uses this mawkish fantasy to tie her shambolic musings into one neat, colorful, hilarious bow.”

criticReviews.author: Ron Fassler (critic)
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Death, Let Me Do My Show’ features the multi-hyphenate actress, writer, composer and comedienne in a very personal, very funny sort of one-person show...Its quickly-paced ninety minutes flew by and once out in the street, audience members like me were still laughing.”

criticReviews.author: Loren Noveck
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s not like we all didn’t learn this lesson in 2020, not like we haven’t all been dancing, fighting, and screaming in the face of death a lot lately. So it’s not like Bloom is taking us to new emotional territory—but she’s holding space for us to work through it with humor and heart. Sometimes that’s good enough.”

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: “Bloom’s grief, while certainly real, sometimes feels secondhand — and her reliance on meta devices never quite give her material either heft or over-the-top hilarity. Still, Bloom is a witty narrator of her journey, quick on her feet with a timely ad-lib”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "The latest Broadway revival, which opened on Sunday at the Hudson Theater, goes wider, a notably rich and mostly successful approach."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Even after nearly three and a half hours of 'Death of a Salesman,' I'd gladly stay longer to watch that story continue."

criticReviews.author: Rob Weinert-Kendt
criticReviews.excerpt: It is not only the casting of the striving Lomans as a Black family that makes this Salesman a departure. It is also that the director, Miranda Cromwell, has rendered much of the play as a dissonant fever dream."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "Ms. Cromwell’s production is, nonetheless, emotionally wrenching as it digs fiercely into the heart of the play."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "The script is unchanged – and surprisingly accommodating to the fresh point of view...infusing the production with a legacy and identity all its own."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "Truly, it’s a rich and moving star performance and the reason to see the show."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s no doubt that casting a Black actor as Willy Loman (for the first time on Broadway, no less) adds a deeper dimension to this monumental role."

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: "The mournful irony Miller built into 'Death of a Salesman' is especially potent now, when our world so often feels as if it’s hanging by a thread. "

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: "As this production makes clear, Miller’s Willy is a more carefully drawn character than that. He’s not simply an avatar for all us little guys."

criticReviews.author: Austin Fimmano
criticReviews.excerpt: "Nearly 80 years after Salesman was first performed, Joe Mantello directs a production that proves the play's sharp thorns have not dulled over time."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "I consider this revival to be the best account of Miller's play I've ever encountered, and the best I'm likely ever to see."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "There's no such thing as a definitive staging of 'Death of a Salesman,' but this version ranks as the finest Broadway production of any classic play in many years."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "Down to the smallest roles, this production is astutely cast, and its arresting design elements add a suitably shabby grandeur to the play’s unsparing view of America’s broken promises."

criticReviews.author: Pete Hempstead
criticReviews.excerpt: "This Death of a Salesman got deep in my bones, and it's been a while since a theatrical experience has given me that powerful emotional response that Aristotle called catharsis."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "'I've seen many productions of this landmark play, but this one stands out for its raw emotional power and its connection to our current national state of disillusionment."

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "That's a reflection on the inherent quality of Arthur Miller's work, that it continues to speak to an audience despite the passage of close to 80 years since it was first presented."

criticReviews.author: Owain Rose
criticReviews.excerpt: Magnificent. If I could give it six stars, I would.

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: ​"Harding gives life to some of the show's finest moments."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "The entire cast is a tasting menu of acting brilliance"

criticReviews.author: Sandy MacDonald
criticReviews.excerpt: Plunkett...superb at juggling moods, from acceptance to profound irritation and back again

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “[Koogler’s] writing radiates a humanity that is a balm for the soul.”

criticReviews.author: Steven Suskin
criticReviews.excerpt: ​"Plunkett's gripping performance is to be expected."

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: "The heart and soul...Maryann Plunkett, who brings a convincing groundedness to her role"

criticReviews.author: Colin Macdonald
criticReviews.excerpt: "The production … is astonishing … as funny as it is deeply moving"

criticReviews.author: Joshua Barone
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: “ ‘Der Rosenkavalier’ is an ensemble opera in which it can be difficult to call anyone a protagonist, but Davidsen’s Marschallin leaves the stage the most evolved.”

criticReviews.author: David Wright
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s great spectacle, but weak drama. And without dramatic credibility, ‘Rosenkavalier’ is reduced to its best bits, a song cycle in costume.”

criticReviews.author: Maya Phillips
criticReviews.excerpt: "Everything is ridiculous, and after an hour and 40 minutes, 'Des Moines', like a night spent drinking at home, ends with a stubborn lack of resolution."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "The emptiness of 'Des Moines' feels as vast and unsettling as its Great Plains setting. Facing up against the cutoff of death, all there is to do is drink and sing and avoid talking about it."

criticReviews.author: Pete Hempstead
criticReviews.excerpt: "I wasn't bored at any time during the play's one hour and 40 minutes. I suspect this was due less to the play itself than to the strength of the performances, all of which end up being as hilarious as they are absurd."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: Making its belated New York premiere, this 2007 drama by the late Denis Johnson, long acclaimed for his novels and short stories, is a kind of dramatic spook house, haunted by the shades of other playwrights' better, more vivid works. It strains to unsettle, using stratagems so well-worn that they have lost the power to provoke. If I had to guess, I'd say that Johnson probably didn't spend much time going to the theatre; if he had, I doubt he would have come up with something as derivative as this.

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "Des Moines sputters at the end...But even if its final destination proves unclear, the rambling journey getting there is infinitely rewarding."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: American author Denis Johnson often wrote about misfits as part of his vision of a semi-mythic West. His play "Des Moines" from 2007, one of seven he wrote, now having its New York premiere at Theatre for a New Audience, includes these themes. The play brings together five unlikely Iowa people for an impromptu party that seems to go off the rails. We are never certain if it’s all a dream or if it really happened. While the cast led by Johanna Day, Arliss Howard and Michael Shannon seem to know what is going on, we the audience are entirely left out of the equation.

criticReviews.author: Holli Harms
criticReviews.excerpt: "The actors are shooting stars. They are comets crisscrossing the stage, tearing it up, and throwing light on one another and the audience."

criticReviews.author: Loren Noveck
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s not really any deeper meaning to be found in one’s cups, here–just momentary camaraderie and some very strange dreams. Maybe that’s the best humanity does have to offer us."

criticReviews.author: Amelia Merrill
criticReviews.excerpt: “On page, it is perfect, but onstage, something is missing.”

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: “There is an interesting play lurking beneath the superficial mockery of Dilaria.”

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: "a stunning exposé of Gen Z 20-year-olds who spend all their free time trolling the Internet"

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "tries to engage the audience in unusual ways. But the execution worked better in previous productions"

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: “Seeing an off-Broadway musical is fun, but it's even more fun to make your own. Hopefully, the kids seeing 'Dog Man' will follow George and Harold's example.”

criticReviews.author: Laurel Graeber
criticReviews.excerpt:
CRITIC'S PICK! "‘Dog Man: The Musical’ Celebrates a Cop Who Sniffs Out Crime.
The bizarro, irreverent world of Dav Pilkey, the creator of the Captain Underpants books, has been deftly translated to the Lucille Lortel Theater’s stage."

criticReviews.author: Mark Dundas Wood
criticReviews.excerpt: "The players all do a fine job. Owen-who barks, yips and howls his spoken lines and lyrics-makes Dog Man a big galumphing sweetheart. Children at the performance under review seemed particularly enamored of Davidson's winsome Li'l Petey. Adults, on the other hand, may take more of a shine to LaVerdiere's scrumptiously villainous big Petey, who is funniest precisely when his attempts at being suave and cool falter-just as with actual felines that scramble to save face after not landing gracefully on all four feet."

criticReviews.author: Dan Rubins
criticReviews.excerpt: A Best Bet "Your Favorite Kid's Favorite Book Come To Life…'Dog Man: The Musical' is structurally sturdy and sophisticated in its storytelling…but also a silly, buoyant burst of energy…that at its heart is about two nutty kids, discovering the joy of live theater for the first time."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Woolfe
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC'S PICK! "Ivo van Hove’s work is smooth, flexible and agile enough to walk the tightrope of any successful “Don Giovanni”: not stinting on the work’s darkness, depth and strangeness, on one hand — and, on the other, not snuffing out its wit, even silliness."

criticReviews.author: Heidi Waleson
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mr. Van Hove’s detailed, intentional directing made the characters and their motivations and interactions leap to the fore. 'Don Giovanni' can feel like a string of unconnected solo turns."

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: A production with promise that would shine more fully with a full creative team.

criticReviews.author: George Grella
criticReviews.excerpt: "Van Hove, a marquee theater director...while his staging supported the form of Don Giovanni, it also stumbled too often in essential places, leaving the music-making alone to carry the success of this performance."

criticReviews.author: David Salazar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Van Hove’s production is not only worth one experience, but multiple to continue discovering the layers and colors of this most fascinating of operas."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Like procedurals, it withholds information to maintain suspense"

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Those sensitive to issues of sexual and child abuse may have some difficulty with Doubt."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Doubt' is an odd kind of mystery, less a whodunit than a wasitdunatall."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "...Doubt is still a sharp and sturdy piece of writing."

criticReviews.author: Vinson Cunningham
criticReviews.excerpt: "At its best, 'Doubt' is about formality."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "...Ryan and Schreiber, presents the play without any intentional new slant on its ideas"

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "...a timely and now seemingly timeless piece of art that shed light"

criticReviews.author: Aramide Tinubu
criticReviews.excerpt: "Liev Schreiber’s performance cuts through a somber and confining single act"

criticReviews.author: Mark Shenton
criticReviews.excerpt: Bruce Norris is following in David Mamet's blistering footsteps to become the current most urgent provocateur of American theatre. That he does so with more humanity and compassion, however, makes his work all the more stinging...'

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: Arch provocateur Bruce Norris returns with a surprisingly sensitive drama about convicted sex offenders... Norris doesn’t ask us to have empathy, but he does make a case for sympathy.'

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: Downstate fulfils art's profound function of making you look and think hard about complex, difficult moral issues that society has a tendency of solving with superficial solutions.'

criticReviews.author: Matt Wolf
criticReviews.excerpt: Controversial but also clear-eyed and compassionate. Bruce Norris's ever-provocative play puts people first, labels second...beautiful and wounding play... in the production of a writer's dreams.'

criticReviews.author: Tim Bano
criticReviews.excerpt: Bruce's norris' harrowing but cynical new play...Downstate has important points to make, and the quality of the production is undeniable. But does it do enough to justify its graphic descriptions...?'

criticReviews.author: Michael Billington
criticReviews.excerpt: ...there is a visceral power to the performances under Pam MacKinnon’s direction. Francis Guinan is outstanding as Fred... Norris has opened up a controversial subject...'

criticReviews.author: Ben Lawrence
criticReviews.excerpt: ... a smart, acutely funny, important piece of work which challenges our never-ending Medieval thirst for revenge.'

criticReviews.author: Henry Hitchings
criticReviews.excerpt: Haunting vision of sex abuse by a playwright with a gift for unsettling...an uncomfortable experience, flecked with humour but bleak and haunting...'

criticReviews.author: Paul Taylor
criticReviews.excerpt: Bruce Norris’s studiedly provocative play... The acting is excellent throughout...I admired, rather than liked the play.'

criticReviews.author: Ann Treneman
criticReviews.excerpt: There are quite a few laughs here amid the pain and anger, but be warned: I was gripped by this play and I wouldn’t want to go again.'

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK "Getting Intimate at ‘Dr. Ride’s American Beach House’: In a witty new play by Liza Birkenmeier, restless friends find themselves challenged by the first American woman in space."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: 4/5 Stars "The route of Birkenmeier’s plot is tightly mapped in retrospect, but full of worthy little detours into character...'Dr. Ride' takes its sweet time to rev up, but it goes the distance when the engine kicks in. It’s a specific and evocative depiction of identity and power at a crossroads."

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: "After 80 luscious minutes of conversation, the company somehow has material for a whole nother play, a ten-minute scorcher between Sally Ride (Sieh) and an old friend Molly (Markey)...The play itself just keeps soaring up and up and up."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "Dr. Ride's American Beach House and the Secret Lives of Lesbians in the 1980s: Sally Ride's historic space journey inspires four women on a St. Louis rooftop."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "A conversation piece for four women who take to a St. Louis rooftop…its air of laziness extends to the playwright, Liza Birkenmeier, who -- despite her knack for distinctive dialogue and a certain offhand, off-the-wall wit -- can't be bothered to come up with anything like drama."

criticReviews.author: Michael Sommers
criticReviews.excerpt: 4/5 Stars: "A sensitive work by an up-and-coming playwright. Ars Nova, a company that discovers and nurtures new artists, adds Birkenmeier's name to the roster of young dramatists whose future plays can be pleasantly anticipated."

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: "Has all the elements of a fascinating drama but as presented by Ars Nova at Greenwich House it is all about subtext and undercurrents which may go right over the heads of many audience members. Little happens but there is much tedious talk which is a cover-up for what goes unsaid."

criticReviews.author: Jacob Horn
criticReviews.excerpt: "Liza Berkenmeier's historically inspired play offers a meditation on queer desire and repression."

criticReviews.author: Linda Buchwald
criticReviews.excerpt: "It's a play that sneaks up on you, lingering long after the lights come up. Even days later I find myself going back to certain scenes. While set at a very specific moment in time, the feelings of being unsatisfied with life are universal."

criticReviews.author: David Roberts
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Dr. Ride's American Beach House' does not rise to an epic tale of 'queer anti-heroes' forging a pathway to self-acceptance and claiming true power and control. Under Katie Brook's direction, the cast does what it can to authenticate their character's conflicts despite the weakness of Liza Birkenmeier's script."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Small, slow and seemingly random, existing almost entirely as subtext…largely about repressed desire….a payoff at the end that might not be enough for many theatergoers…yet, there are many moments where we feel encouraged to bask in their friendship."

criticReviews.author: Joe Belfatti
criticReviews.excerpt: "Birkenmeier's play bravely imagines what it was like when being gay involved claustrophobic secrets, blind struggle and a stepping into the void to create a reality without social or cultural precedence."

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: “This stirring tragedy gives a voice to the voiceless: not just the unfairly treated Semmelweis, but the women whose pain was ignored, and whose deaths were dismissed as routine.”

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: “The ending is rushed and clumsy but it doesn’t matter. One of our finest, alchemically instinctive actors is back where he belongs: onstage.”

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mark Rylance is astonishing – again – in this unsettling, atmospheric drama about the downfall of a pioneering doctor"

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "Playing a maverick doctor who discovers a ground-breaking cure, the star embodies crusading eccentricity – and dangerous monomania... [this play places] resonant emphasis on the dangers of group-think and the way medical hierarchies can crush whistleblowers. "

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: “He [Rylance] makes Semmelweis hard to like. But he also lets you see inside his head, showing the thrill of being part of a new way of thinking, indicating  the panic as he half realises his mind is becoming disturbed. It’s an extraordinarily subtle and emotional performance.”

criticReviews.author: Dave Fargnoli
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mark Rylance gives a fascinating, febrile performance in this unwieldy but absorbing historical drama."

criticReviews.author: Greg Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: Dr Semmelweis is utterly fascinating in every respect, especially as it unearths such a vital piece of forgotten, or ignored, history.  As a pioneer of medicine, Mark Rylance leads an impressive cast in this gripping historical drama.

criticReviews.author: Dominic Maxwell
criticReviews.excerpt: “There is humour here as well as physical theatre, music, anger, sadness, emotional nuance.”

criticReviews.author: Tim Bano
criticReviews.excerpt: “Everything about the production seems designed to make you feel like you’ve had an exhilarating night at the theatre, while not wholly delivering it. It’s the trappings without the substance; many hands, making effortful work.”

criticReviews.author: Demetrios Matheou
criticReviews.excerpt: “This new play, written by Stephen Brown with Rylance...is a perplexing animal – passionate, instructive, imaginatively directed, but also sometimes stilted and, at its heart, lacking the nuanced characterisation we have come to expect from its star.”

criticReviews.author: Sophie Luck
criticReviews.excerpt: “The madness of genius can be a blessing and a curse. For ‘Dr Semmelweis,’ it led to a tragic and tortured end but his story is now being told and getting the respect a man who saved the lives of millions of women and babies always deserved. This riveting and revolutionary play is one not to miss!”

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: "explosively funny satire about the end of the world"

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "if this show is anything, it is fun."

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Steve Coogan impresses but it’s oddly stolid"

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s entertaining but never quite as savage as you expect."

criticReviews.author: Dave Fargnoli
criticReviews.excerpt: “Steve Coogan displays impeccable comic timing”

criticReviews.author: Alice Saville
criticReviews.excerpt: "Comedy famously ages badly but the humour here is evergreen"

criticReviews.author: Claire Allfree
criticReviews.excerpt: "Steve Coogan steals the show but can’t save it"

criticReviews.author: Rachel Halliburton
criticReviews.excerpt: "It's when playing Dr Strangelove that Coogan truly takes off"

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: “For the show to really work, it needs more moments like that one: simple, goofy and fast. That last quality is important in farce, but unfortunately, in this case, the second half of the evening drags a bit. Some scenes even slow down enough to suggest … emotions? In this context, that’s just like garlic to a vampire.”

criticReviews.author: Kyle Turner
criticReviews.excerpt: “The show makes it difficult to begrudge pointing out the occasional imprecise, maybe, I’ll say it, potentially transphobic ‘man in a dress’ nature to some of the jokes because, after all, it advertises itself as a gender-bending reenvisioning of the text.”

criticReviews.author: Raven Snook
criticReviews.excerpt: "4/5 - 'Dracula, A Comedy of Terrors' goes for the jocular. Gordon Greenberg and Steve Rosen's silly, sexy spoof of Bram Stoker's bloodcurdling novel replaces horror with humor, centering on a pumped-up, preening, pansexual vampire who is suffering through an eternal-life crisis."

criticReviews.author: Harry Haun
criticReviews.excerpt: “A funny thing happened to Arnie Burton on the way to ‘Dracula: A Comedy of Terrors,’ a raucous little spook spoof now at New World Stages. For several decades, Burton has been practicing—and perfecting—comedy on the stages of New York...’Dracula: A Comedy of Terrors’ is a relatively light sentence for Burton in that regard. The script by Steve Rosen and director Gordon Greenberg only allots him two characters to play, both women.”

criticReviews.author: Christian Lewis
criticReviews.excerpt: “I don’t believe the play is actually trying to say much of anything about sexuality as much as it is just trying to be sexy– and it does that very well. While this may not be the truest or most cerebral adaptation of ‘Dracula,’ it is certainly the gayest and campiest version I’ve ever seen, and one that I’d like to think Bram Stoker (who is widely believed to have been queer) would’ve enjoyed.”

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “The tone is struck at the top, when we are told, ‘Rest assured, you will be horrified. One way or another.’ After that, merriment prevails, thanks to a company willing to deliver the ripest nonsense with the straightest of faces while leaping in and out of assorted roles like decathlon runners. Not since The Mystery of Irma Vep has the supernatural been taken for such a wild comic ride.”

criticReviews.author: Melissa Rose Bernardo
criticReviews.excerpt: “If you’re expecting historical accuracy, you’ve come to the wrong place...you probably never thought you’d get a straight-up comic take on the century-plus-old story.”

criticReviews.author: Sandy MacDonald
criticReviews.excerpt: “No amount of description can convey the delights of this ingenious rejiggering. You may gasp, you may marvel, but mostly you’ll be too busy laughing — thanks to all the artistry brought into play.”

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: Each generation gets its own version of Bram Stoker’s "Dracula," the classic vampire horror story, that possibly reflects the needs of its own time. The latest version now called "Dracula: A Comedy of Terrors" by Gordon Greenberg and Steve Rosen is a hoot, both a parody and a comedy, a cross-dressing hilarity in the style of both Charles Ludlam’s Ridiculous Theatrical Company and Monty Python. A fabulously talented cast of five led by buff, sexy young James Daly in the title role get a workout with the other four playing many roles in quick costume changes. Greenberg’s production with its witty script and design makes this a must-see entertainment. After the pandemic and other recent horrors, this is just what the doctor ordered.

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: “In the case of Dracula, ‘A Comedy of Terrors,’ now at New World Stages, there’s very little chance you’ll die of fright. However, you may die laughing during its 90-minute run. Of course, you won’t want to expire until the show is over so you can savor every moment of the deliciously irreverent script by Steve Rosen and Gordon Greenberg. It oh-so-cleverly mixes elements of Bram Stoker’s classic vampire novel with anachronistic, up-to-the-minute updates for maximum hilarity.”

criticReviews.author: Margret Echeverria
criticReviews.excerpt: "This is how comedy is done!  No tripping into traps here.  Run to see this show and treat yourself this Halloween season, Kids."

criticReviews.author: Elyse Trevers
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show is a fun, pleasant jaunt with wordplay and some popular cultural references. Just a little something to sink your teeth into."

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt:
Before it became known as a vehicle for strippers and baggy pants comics, burlesque meant parodies of well-known plays and musical theatre. And that latter meaning perfectly applies to Dracula: A Comedy of Terrors, Gordon Greenberg and Steve Rosen’s comic bite out of Bram Stoker’s 1897 vampire novel, Dracula. It was first dramatized in 1924, seven years before it became a classic horror film starring Romanian-born actor Bela Lugosi, who gained fame for his stage portrayal of the bloodsucking Transylvanian count. Dracula has been the red meat inspiring numerous vampire movies and plays, some intended to make us howl with fright, others to make us gurgle with laughter. The last local attempt came just before the pandemic hit, with Kate Hammill’s Dracula, which I reviewed here.

Dracula: A Comedy of Terrors, the story’s most recent spoof, at New World Stages, cunningly directed by coauthor Greenberg, does a bloody good job of satirizing the original in the anything goes style of the late Charles Ludlam’s Ridiculous Theatrical Company. The production is more technically polished than most of what Ludlam provided, and its small cast of five, each—except for James Daly as Dracula—playing multiple roles, is every bit as intelligently funny as Ludlam’s crew, knowing just what twists to make in speaking lines or carrying out physical actions in order to suck as much hilarity from them as possible.

Performed in a unit set...with gloomily gothic features...this fangs-in-cheek takeoff allows its thespians to have the time of their lives (and deaths). Only rarely winking at the audience..., the incisive actors sink their incisors into the flesh of their material with perfect sangfroid, keeping their characters grounded no matter how batty their behavior.

criticReviews.author: Darryl Reilly
criticReviews.excerpt: The youthful and sensual James Daly’s Ortonesque characterization as the ideal vampire Count is the centerpiece of this comically sexy spoof. A seasoned and animated quartet all gleefully mug their way through their multiple campy Charles Ludlam-type roles with elan during this breezy presentation. It is an accomplished 90-minute diversion inciting abundant audience laughter.

criticReviews.author: Stanford Friedman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Utilizing elements of romantic comedy, farce, puppetry and high camp, playwrights Gordon Greenberg and Steve Rosen serve up a confection that is keenly unwrapped by an ensemble cast of five."

criticReviews.author: Olivia Rook
