It is, quite simply, magic...The script is both sharp and masterfully structured...Thorne's writing is leavened not only with emotion, but also with great humour...A deeply theatrical experience, a love letter to theatre itself...Full of literal magic...This pure delight...makes this eighth story in the ‘Harry Potter’ series a very particular experience.”

criticReviews.author: Michael Billington
criticReviews.excerpt: “A thrilling theatrical spectacle…I got as much pleasure from the staging as from the convoluted story. Tiffany and his designer, Christine Jones, have created magic out of the simplest ingredients…Any danger that the effects would upstage the actors is overcome by a set of strong performances…While it helps to be a paid-up Potterhead, Tiffany and his team stage the piece with such dazzling assurance that I finally began to see the point of being wild about Harry.”

criticReviews.author: Sarah Hemming
criticReviews.excerpt: “Thrilling: gripping, dark, wittily acted and often visually dazzling. Above all, though, it succeeds because the team has put transformation right at the heart of the story, both structurally and emotionally. It’s a move that allows the drama to play to drama’s strengths...Overall, this is a triumph. For a bunch of muggles, the creative team has certainly brewed up a wizard show."

criticReviews.author: Maxie Szalwinska
criticReviews.excerpt: "Delivers in spades for more fanatical 'Potter' followers, while the theatrical wizardry will make sure everyone else is happy to go along on the five-hour-plus ride. It’s worth mentioning, though, that some familiarity with, and affection for, the books will guarantee a bigger emotional return...It’s the unostentatious yet beguiling visual touches in Tiffany’s production that give this epic lift-off...The show appeals broadly at first, piercingly later, to grown-ups and children alike."

criticReviews.author: Jack Shepherd
criticReviews.excerpt: “A theatre production of immense wonder...Truly magical...This tale focuses on themes of friendship and family, developing both new and old characters in a meaningful and believable way...Part one was a jubilant ride...The second part is an emotional rollercoaster that sees the story progress through what will no doubt be quite a controversial storyline...A spectacle for the theatre, one that is filled to the brim with fan service and magical imagery that will amaze...A fantastic experience.”

criticReviews.author: Henry Hitchings
criticReviews.excerpt: “For once the so-called theatrical event of the year really is just that…Packed with pathos, dazzling choreography and moments of pure enchantment…John Tiffany’s finely orchestrated production is often gorgeous…If explaining the story’s more ticklish details sometimes stalls its momentum, the characterization is richly convincing…For the legions of Pottermaniacs eager to be reunited with the characters they adore, this will be a magical experience."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: “Rau reveals the eagerness of audiences to be led, even to the most unspeakable acts of violence.”

criticReviews.author: Tony Marinelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "Hate Radio" operates as both a scrupulous act of historical excavation and a theatrical indictment.

criticReviews.author: Brittany Crowell
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s haunting how normal their messaging may sound even as they are calling for the deaths of hundreds of thousands.”

criticReviews.author: Deirdre Donovan
criticReviews.excerpt: The RTLM radio station in Rwanda proves that words can kill.

criticReviews.author: JK Clarke
criticReviews.excerpt: "Hate Radio has the dubious distinction of being, simultaneously, a play you should see and one you probably don’t want to experience."

criticReviews.author: Ben Brantley
criticReviews.excerpt: "Feels as timid and awkward as the new kid on the first day of school...'Head Over Heels' lacks the courage of its contradictions. It mutters deferentially when what you want is a rebel yell...What’s lacking in the musical performances here is the go-for-broke exuberance that made the Go-Go’s so irresistible...Its audience might leave the theater less hungry if this oddly earnest show could really kick up its heels and let the message take care of itself."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "To enjoy 'Head Over Heels,' which offers quite a lot to enjoy, it is probably best to kick up your heels and put your head on hold. That’s not to say that this saucy, boisterous musical doesn’t have a brainy side, starting with its ambitious crossbreeding of four time periods...But at heart the show is a campy romp...Broadway traditionalists may not approve, but that feels like part of the point...A fantasy and celebration of nonconformity, and it puts its casting where its mouth is."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "If the premise of 'Head Over Heels' sounds a little nutso, that’s because the show is a lot nutso, in the most delightfully daffy, exuberantly heart-open way...'Head Over Heels' is joyfully queering the canon (which isn’t all that straight to begin with) and throwing a heady, hearty party while it’s at it...Part of the appeal of 'Head Over Heels' is that while it’s got Broadway sparkle to it, it depends almost entirely on its ensemble to generate its goofy, big-hearted brand of magic."

criticReviews.author: Michael Schulman
criticReviews.excerpt: “A bouncy, bizarro, occasionally didactic musical...The amalgam is so brazen as to be immediately disarming: it would take a truly bad sport not to get on board with ersatz Elizabethan verse side by side with eighties earworms, delivered with equal gusto by a game cast...Mayer’s production revels in postmodern whimsy...The familiar tunes give the tale a welcome infusion of nostalgia...but the catalogue is puddle-deep."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "The book is still a sophomoric mess, and the 17 songs, which are mostly either fast or rather less so, are lively but unvaried...Michael Mayer has done what he can to put a directorial shine on 'Head Over Heels'...Everyone else in the cast takes care of business, and if you really, really like the Go-Go’s, you might possibly find the results tolerable."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Head Over Heels' just strikes as winking and self-satisfied, occasionally amusing, occasionally cloying...For a show that is so determined to transcend convention, 'Head Over Heels' feels predicable from start to finish...'Head Over Heels' offers up a few surprises...But the biggest surprise is an unfortunate one: The Go-Go’s songs don’t hold up all that well."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "An over-written, over-designed, and generally overdone production...Thanks, no doubt, to the Oracle of Delphi (played here by the impishly funny Peppermint), it’s a miracle that at least some of the wit in Jeff Whitty’s original book gets through...The show never recovers from the pervasive feeling of exhaustion. There’s the exertion of making the stilted Spencer Liff choreography seem vaguely vogue. There’s the constant struggle to push and shove songs into places where they don’t fit."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "Relentlessly frothy musical...You'll either find the humor uproarious fun or, like me, an utter trial...The performers certainly give the material their all...Mayer's blithe staging keeps things moving at a fast pace...Despite the ample professionalism on display, the show comes across as painfully strained rather than pleasurably antic. 'Head Over Heels' may be admirably woke when it comes to gender fluidity, but as entertainment, it's strictly retrograde."

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "While the dialogue has occasional pop, it’s the performances that keep the show rolling"

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Director Gordon Greenberg’s production is eager to sweep you up in its bright lights"

criticReviews.author: Regina Robbins
criticReviews.excerpt: "Squeeze your memories into spandex and get ready to turn back the clock."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "The Heart of Rock and Roll is the funniest new musical of the season"

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "...funny, unpretentious ’80s fun"

criticReviews.author: Frank Rizzo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Humor and brightness is what fuels this engine"

criticReviews.author: Kenji Fujishima
criticReviews.excerpt: "...I came out feeling buzzed, entertained…and slightly ashamed"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: Stop the presses! The headline news of the day is The Heart of Rock and Roll is...not bad.

criticReviews.author: Caroline Cao
criticReviews.excerpt: "The production’s most critical visual undoing is leaving the scenic design — and Veronica, for that matter — physically unblemished by a near-catastrophe after the smoke has passed"

criticReviews.author: Raven Snook
criticReviews.excerpt: "4/5 Stars! Lick it up, baby: The high-school-is-hell musical Heathers is back to take another shot at being popular."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "The score is so vigorous and the emotional logic of Heathers is so rickety, it’s like using a Ferrari engine to power a Citi Bike."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Beyond its sociological themes, Heathers is a ton of stylish, well-crafted fun with top-notch acting and top-to-bottom earworms."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "A musical that absolutely anticipated the loop of opportunism and cynicism that has led to so much social breakdown over the last decade."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "Those girls should check their makeup; they're looking awfully tired."

criticReviews.author: Howard Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: ""It's a raucous and thoroughly smashing homecoming for the old Westerberg High School gang as the nerds, jocks, clueless staff, and a trio of very mean girls gather for a top-notch revival of Heathers"

criticReviews.author: Victor Gluck
criticReviews.excerpt: "cult show "Heathers the Musical" is back, bigger and better than ever in a revised version"

criticReviews.author: Ben Brantley
criticReviews.excerpt: "Foulmouthed, electrically tuneful and furiously funny, with explicit descriptions of its title character’s bungled sex-change operation and erotic adventures, “Hedwig” developed a cult following that kept it running off Broadway for two years, with subsequent production around the world."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Mitchell juices his 1998 script with topical jabs: dating sites, TMZ and Mark Rylance. Director Michael Mayer expertly balances the needs of a messy, punk protest with jaw-dropping visuals."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "The enormous scale and professionalism of Michael Mayer’s production cuts two ways. It seems to think it’s a work of glam philosophy: part Rocky Horror, part Plato’s Symposium. But musicals do  better to bury their abstractions, not animate and project them on scrims, however beautifully. Happily, Hedwig is plenty touching — and fun — most of the time."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "Transformation is tricky, sometimes even painful. But Broadway’s sensational “Hedwig and the Angry Inch” is a reminder that change doesn’t have to hurt. This raucous pop-rock musical — a show with proudly ratty downtown roots and rabid fans — survives and thrives uptown."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "A spectacular revival...a rock concert with political as well as psychosexual overtones. What fun! ...The band may be wearing fashionable glam-rock costumes rather than ripped T-shirts and shredded jeans and safety pins in their nostrils, but the music (and the anger fueling it) is closer to punk rock and more in step with Hedwig’s nihilist inclinations."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "As to the question of how the scrappy, subversive 1998 cult performance piece about gender identity, transformation and pop mythology would sit on Broadway, the show, its protagonist and her pulse-pounding band tear up the Belasco stage like they own it. If screaming rock concert-style veneration is not your thing, stay home."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: If your memory of this brilliant 1998 rock musical is that it works best in a grungy joint, ideally where the floors are sticky, the seats half-empty and the air heavy with tragedy, there is much about director Michael Mayer's new Broadway production to pull you up short...Hedwig, you might say, has emerged triumphant after all these years of graft and toil."

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "“Hedwig” is a tricky animal: Framed like a concert, it requires a charismatic lead who can go wild during the most raucous numbers, but also handle long, narrative banter between the songs — and the occasional audience interaction."

criticReviews.author: Ben Brantley
criticReviews.excerpt: "The sexiest couple on a New York stage just now...I groaned when I heard 'Heisenberg' was traveling to Broadway. I would never have predicted that it would seem even more vibrant and emotionally charged...The production’s creative team thwarts expectations at every turn...Mr. Stephens is an uncannily subtle dramatist who never wears his depths on the surface...He makes us see how conventional story lines fail to hold their shape when unspooled within the mess of human reality."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "If I understand the oblique title correctly, 'Heisenberg' is about how being with another person—being observed, at close range—can affect your direction...Mark Brokaw’s spare production seems even less imposing in the company's Broadway house, but that works to its advantage. Stephens’s carefully crafted 75-minute play has a sense of how little its characters matter to the universe. It makes that smallness feel liberating."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "One of last year’s best dramas has somehow become one of this year’s best comedies...The two-person cast is still terrific, with Parker doing her best stage work in years, and Arndt again a wonderful surprise to New York audiences. The script, too, is all but unaltered...Yet somehow the spin seems to have reversed direction; it’s now less like a whirlpool pulling you under than a tornado flinging you up...But with the story’s increased size come the social pleasures of large-scale theater."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "It is blush-makingly trite...The result is, not to put too fine a point on it, a blatant exercise in masculine wish fulfillment, and it doesn’t help that Ms. Parker seems to think that Georgie is an inexplicably youthful Manic Pixie Dream Girl..Mr. Stephens has aided and abetted Ms. Parker by putting eye-rollingly twee sentences in Georgie’s mouth that no actor, however talented, should be expected to utter with a straight face. He’s the culprit-in-chief—she’s merely a co-conspirator."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: “Mary-Louise Parker and Denis Arndt and this wonderful play have made the transition with deeper performances, even with the volume turned up a notch to accommodate the bigger space. It is, hands down, the most romantic, not to mention sexiest, show in town…The acting is stripped bare as, in the beautifully calibrated performances, Alex’s initial imperturbability yields to Georgie’s ever-more poignant persistence.”

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "For Mary-Louise Parker die-hards, 'Heisenberg' won’t disappoint...There’s fertile material there, along with moments that are lovely and contrived in director Mark Brokaw’s spare staging. But the issue with the play remains unchanged from last year’s Off-Broadway run. Arndt lives his role. Parker plays hers. There’s a nagging difference, that’s for certain."

criticReviews.author: Breanne L. Heldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Despite moving to a larger venue, the play is nothing if not intimate...Brokaw’s production itself is wisely bare-bones...The emphasis should be on these two opposites finding something intangible that they’re each missing, and any further frills might distract from that. Stephens’ script is jammed with insightful, unforgettable lines...The show has just enough comedy sprinkled throughout to keep the audience laughing and leave them with plenty to ponder."

criticReviews.author: Matt Windman
criticReviews.excerpt: "In all its nakedness, Brokaw’s production resembles an acting class, where only a table and chairs would be available to suggest a setting. As it happens, the play itself is just as thin as the production values...Despite its initial promise, this static two-hander quickly goes flat. Nevertheless, Parker and Arndt play off each other wonderfully. Parker is a wild bundle of energy and whimsy, while Arndt, initially the straight man to Parker’s theatrics, eventually opens up and comes to life."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Peters makes it clear that Dolly is talking about real hardships...She sings the Jerry Herman songs thrillingly, of course...I don’t mean that she isn’t funny; she is...The other new principals match the bright polish of the original cast, which has grown a bit zany with time...Ms. Peters goes along with all this, to a point. But sometimes I felt she would rather observe the parade than be in it. Personally, I’m a sucker for that: I think it gives this 'Dolly' a fascinating new valence."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “A blissful Broadway revival…The part of Dolly is exquisitely suited to Midler’s enormous warmth, savvy and drive. It’s hard to imagine a better match of actor and role: It is, in a word, perfection…‘Hello, Dolly!’ may be a vehicle for its star, but this revival treats it like a vintage Rolls-Royce. From the rousing overture on, everything about the production, directed with joyful aplomb by Jerry Zaks, gleams with old-fashioned charm…Jerry Herman’s exuberant score is a show-tune bonanza.”

criticReviews.author: Hilton Als
criticReviews.excerpt: "The characters address the audience from time to time, which gives Midler a chance to connect with us by drawing on who she really is, as well as whom she wants to portray...The role of Dolly isn’t necessarily tailor-made for Midler—she’s infinitely more complicated and funny and there isn’t a corny bone in her body—but she has remade the character in her own image: as a scrappy trickster with needs and vulnerabilities."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: “Ms. Midler’s singing voice is in a desperate, sometimes shocking state of disrepair…As for the rest of the performance, Ms. Midler doesn’t even bother to act…She can’t dance and isn’t funny…David Hyde Pierce is all wrong as Horace…What’s more, he and Ms. Midler have no romantic chemistry at all, which makes the show even less dramatically plausible...Every supporting performance is a grotesque caricature…As for the musical numbers, they’re camped up to the hilt.”

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "Murphy is absolutely wonderful as the meddling, multitasking matchmaker...Murphy’s Dolly is gabby, game and gleeful as she dispenses the pleasures of Jerry Herman’s songs and Michael Stewart’s lines...Jerry Zaks’ production is better. The dancing of Warren Carlyle’s choreography is sharper and funnier. The sound is more crisp, the ensemble more assured and the accompanying stars perfectly aligned."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "The two-time Tony winner brings high spirits, warmth and a voice that will make you laugh and cry with joy...Victor Garber is gruff and blustering...Molly Griggs lends humor as straight-laced hat-shop girl Minnie Fae and London star Charlie Stemp lights up the stage with his bright smile and brilliant dancing feet as boyish clerk Barnaby...With the terrific current cast, wall-to-wall musical gems and ace dancing, design and direction, it remains a star vehicle that purrs."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "This Dolly’s personal style is to twinkle and charm people into getting her way. She also has the acting chops to moisten eyeballs when she entreats her late husband to bless her renouncement of widowhood...A new addition to the cast, Charlie Stemp, seems a bit too broad in the comic role of Cornelius’s sidekick...As usually happens when a director and a choreographer keep a sharp eye on their baby, the overall production of this classic never looked better."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "The two-time Tony Award winning performer has brought a poignancy to the production that wasn't quite in evidence with her predecessor...Which is not to say that she falls short of the role's comedic demands. Her performance is less vivacious than Midler's, but no less hilarious...If Garber's more restrained performance is less gut-busting, it's also less of a caricature...Stemp is a revelation...Zaks' perfectly tooled staging hasn't lost a step, dancing or otherwise, since the show opened."

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: "this roof-raising musical spectacular is the show of the year"

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Imelda Staunton sparkles in this effervescent revival"

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Imelda Staunton plays the matchmaker with stunning results"

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "The star raises the roof without breaking into a sweat"

criticReviews.author: Alice Saville
criticReviews.excerpt: "Imelda Staunton brings heart and substance to this lavish feast"

criticReviews.author: Holly O'Mahony
criticReviews.excerpt: "Hello, Dolly! has to be one of the most uncomplicatedly ebullient musicals"

criticReviews.author: Rachel Halliburton
criticReviews.excerpt: "Imelda Staunton is luminous in a joyful revival"

criticReviews.author: Lucinda Everett
criticReviews.excerpt: "No whacky modern retellings or modest sets here. This is giddy, Golden-age glitz."

criticReviews.author: David Nice
criticReviews.excerpt: "Operettaish bitter-sweetness raised to the sublime in a miracle of perfect timing"

criticReviews.author: Caroline McGinn
criticReviews.excerpt: "Imelda Staunton will blow your socks off with this terrifically entertaining revival"

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: “Though not perfectly told, Ali’s discovery that art is love, with or without the guy, is too rich not to reach a bigger audience, and a million more girls on fire.”

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "CRITIC’S PICK:...easily stands out as one of the rare must-sees in a crowded season."

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: “Though ‘Hell's Kitchen’ takes plenty of liberties with Keys's life, to the credit of her and bookwriter Kristoffer Diaz, it's not a highlight reel. The creators don't sugarcoat the low notes of Keys's adolesence: her younger self's willfulness to a fault, the illness of her mentor, and gravest of all, the overpolicing of her community, filled with artists of color.”

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Alicia Keys musical is on fire with powerhouse performances"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Hell’s Kitchen is ultimately a celebration of the city—and the people who make it pop."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Hell’s Kitchen’ is a mother-daughter story...They take Keys’s remarkable solo work and fill it out, expanding its feeling of context and community. A jukebox plays what you’ve heard before, and though ‘Hell’s Kitchen’ is unquestionably a slick commercial machine, it’s also, with admirable frequency, able to pull off the feat of making the musically familiar feel brand new.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "worth being wary of any musical that positions itself as a love letter to New York City."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: “While ‘Hell’s Kitchen’ is musically ravishing—the musical, named after the New York neighborhood in which Ms. Keys grew up, is more slender dramatically. The book, by Kristoffer Diaz, curves along formulaic grooves, even if they closely track Ms. Keys’s life.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "A thoughtful, beautifully acted new play...directed with assurance by Kate Whoriskey...Mr. Pierce’s characters are superbly drawn, his dialogue smooth and smart. He’s a promising writer...But the plotting of 'Her Requiem' becomes a little baggy...From this point the play becomes diffuse, a quilt of underdeveloped subplots."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Contrived and gently pretentious, Greg Pierce’s 'Her Requiem' is the Off Broadway equivalent of a 'New Yorker' short story...Characters are improbably glib yet earnest; moral stakes are real but unfrightening; the tone is bittersweet puzzlement...Pierce raises several questions over 90 minutes, few of which he answers to satisfaction...The acting is strong, with Friedman and Winningham—two of New York’s finest character actors—touchingly torn between protecting their child and their marriage."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "Greg Pierce’s well-written but ineffectual play about a teenage wunderkind whose miraculous musical genius turns her home life upside-down and inspires a morbid death cult....After introducing the characters and giving us some background on how everyone got here, the playwright seems at a loss...The only tension in the air is between Caitlin's warring parents, who at least argue with intelligence and some eloquence."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "While it boasts strong performances and pungent dialogue, 'Her Requiem' fails to make much narrative or thematic sense...Besides that absurd plot device, the playwright fumbles the ball with his characterizations...Director Kate Whoriskey...is unable to lend much coherence to the emotionally scattered proceedings. Nor are the performers, although such veterans as Friedman, Winningham and Van Patten deliver their usual unimpeachable work."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "A fascinating look at the fine line between commitment and obsession, practicality and philistinism...Director Kate Whoriskey hits all the right notes, a happy meeting of smart design and layered performances...Winningham and Friedman have a believable chemistry...Pierce probingly explores our tendency to see our own issues in a great work of art, even if those themes weren't intended by the artist."

criticReviews.author: Michael Dale
criticReviews.excerpt: "A solid production by director Kate Whoriskey, but Pierce's promising text could use some consistency of tone. The play seems somewhat satirical at first, which undercuts the moments of discomforting reality between Caitlin and Tommy, who may or may not be aware of his predatory manipulations...A variation of the stage-mother scenario,'Requiem' has some interesting ideas that haven't quite coalesced yet, but with Winningham and Friedman at the center, the piece certainly intrigues."

criticReviews.author: Matthew Murray
criticReviews.excerpt: "Little of what he's built captures your imagination, or for that matter your attention...The surprises and misdirections that crop up along the way, as everyone begins jockeying for position closest to Caitlin's gaze, are compelling. Not much else, however...Further, tone problems are rampant...Aside from Winningham, the acting is uneven, too."

criticReviews.author: Deirdre Donovan
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Her Requiem' is hardly flawless, but Pierce hits some right notes. Its characters are intriguingly if perhaps way too off-beat. And if does pose some interesting questions about artists, art, and what price a young artist like Caitlin — and her family — must pay before a work emerges into the light."

criticReviews.author: Tulis McCall
criticReviews.excerpt: "Greg Pierce writes a wandering path that leads to the showdown, and these actors bring their A-game all the way through...In the end, it comes down to the two men battling it out...[but] it is the women who sort through the ballast in this tale. It just takes the author a long time to get us there. Next outing we would all be okay with getting there sooner and opening up the gates leading out of archetypes into the unknown."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Improbable if skillfully acted new drama....The play takes a couple of even more unexpected turns. I won’t spoil them except to say that they feel imposed by the playwright, in order to goose up an otherwise tame story, and to make it more thought provoking...Pierce can thank director Kate Whoriskey for assembling a first-class design team and a group of actors who, by their very presence nearly guarantee something worth watching."

criticReviews.author: Janice C. Simpson
criticReviews.excerpt: "Some of this is improbable, not to mention a little melodramatic, but director Kate Whoriskey has put together an elegant production. I wanted to move right into the comfortable home that set designer Derek McLane has created for the family. And the casting couldn't be better....But it's all a little too much for a 90-minute play. 'Her Requiem' is ambitious but it both overpromises and underperforms."

criticReviews.author: Carey Purcell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Life is mirroring art, which is mirroring life, in 'Her Requiem', the ambitious new play by Greg Pierce...'Her Requiem' addresses various intriguing ideas...but their execution lacks coherence at times...At the conclusion of the play, Caitlin’s requiem is completed, but the audience only hears the first chords. It seems an appropriate metaphor for this play which, with a few rewrites and sharpened focus, could be quite excellent."

criticReviews.author: Olivia Rook
criticReviews.excerpt: "Brady shows off his powerful vocals in the rousing solo numbers...and athletically tackles the tightly choreographed number 'One Last Hope' with ceaseless energy."

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "The show chugs along agreeably enough, powered by the attitude and powerhouse vocals of the Muses."

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Perhaps this musical shows the film’s age: this feels like old-school Disney, its hero not quite self-mocking enough."

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Still, it’s hard to work up much enthusiasm about Casey Nicholaw’s musclebound production."

criticReviews.author: Alice Saville
criticReviews.excerpt: "Unfortunately, there’s none of the same imaginative energy in this stodgy new stage version."

criticReviews.author: Sam Marlowe
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s not much more to it, but as far as it goes, it’s amiable fun."

criticReviews.author: Greg Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: It’s a show that embraces its mythological roots with a wink and a smile, delivering a thunderously entertaining evening. Hercules is a heroic hit, complete with tunics, thunderbolts, and toe-tapping tunes.

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Here Lies Love’ bets that glamour can make up for narrative — or, rather, that in a show about the dangers of political demagogy, glamour itself is the narrative. It’s a case of form follows function into the fire. We are drawn to cultural and political excitement in much the same, often dangerous way.”

criticReviews.author: Allison Considine
criticReviews.excerpt: “Audience members whose knowledge of Imelda Marcos is limited to the fact that she owned 3,000 pairs of shoes will only leave with a partial understanding of this violent period. The musical has no book, and the punchy songs paint broad strokes of the 60-year history... Still, this rollicking, form-breaking musical party is well worth an RSVP.”

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “Our complicity with such cycles of populist fervor—whether, depending on your ticket, as spectators from a safe distance or as extras in a mob scene—is the loudly beating heart of ‘Here Lies Love,’ a party that hides a mordant critique of civilization and its discotheques.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “...the crowd itself is ‘Here Lies Love’s’ main character, this mass of people looking to be appeased by a good performance, no matter who’s singing the political karaoke. The show ends with democracy, but it has a wary relationship with the masses. The thought may be that, lured by a beat good enough, they’ll dance along to anything.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: “What may be most remarkable about ‘Here Lies Love’ is how deftly it pivots from the celebratory and even sentimental presentation of Imelda’s rise to the inevitably condemnatory”

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: “The real pull of ‘Here Lies Love’ is the staging, with a malleable performance space, an audience herded to and fro, and cast members finding perches throughout the venue.”

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: “You can sit and observe the show all around you or you can pay to hit the orchestra floor and party with the Marcoses. Whee!...At no more than 100 minutes long, ‘Here Lies Love’ never over-indulges nor does it lose the audience’s attention for a moment. “

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: “Byrne and Fatboy Slim’s sung-through score is the star of the 90-minute production, a hypnotic churn of synth beats, funky rhythms and pop momentum that aims squarely for the pelvis.”

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: “A testament as much as a play, it is a stark and compelling piece of work and a bold statement of intent"

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: “This 90-minute show bites off more than it can chew but that is not necessarily a weakness.”

criticReviews.author: Anya Ryan
criticReviews.excerpt: "Despite its subject matter, the play feels sterile, cold and emotionally airless"

criticReviews.author: Dominic Maxwell
criticReviews.excerpt: “The impact is every bit as awful as it needs to be.”

criticReviews.author: Matthew Plampton
criticReviews.excerpt: “This is essential theatre: a production that reminds us of the importance of critical thinking, of sitting with discomfort, and of refusing to shy away from difficult questions; for to do otherwise can lead to devastating consequences.”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK: “ ‘Here We Are’ is as experimental as Sondheim throughout his career wanted everything to be...We, too, will always want more, even when we’ve had what by any reasonable standards should already be more than enough.”

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: “Considering that it’s the final musical by the renowned composer-lyricist who died in 2021, Stephen Sondheim’s ‘Here We Are’ was guaranteed to jolt. Although the show emerges as modestly engaging, it adds a zap of electricity to the theatre season, thanks to inspired work by a dream cast and ace designers who serve up a slim slice of surrealism under Joe Mantello's ('Wicked') direction.”

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Here We Are’ is more broadly funny than the films and also more overtly philosophical, with a recurring theme about the gap between appearances and reality—though it doesn’t go all that deep.”

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Here We Are’ is torn between its reasonable desire to obliterate its characters and its aspiration, if not quite to save them, then to remain open-ended as to where they—and we—go from here. If it’s sometimes a muddled impulse, it’s also a humane one. Sondheim certainly didn’t go gentle into the apocalypse of late capitalism, but he didn’t go heartless either. He stayed complicated. He gave us more to see.”

criticReviews.author: Naveen Kumar
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Here We Are’ delights in the flavor of its vapid jet-sets, but ultimately spits them out in a resolution that betrays its own internal logic. It’s too much, and robs the show of its potential teeth. Better to know when the feast is done.”

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: “What music there is, is playful and joyous. You wish there were more of it, especially a finale. But Ives and Mantello do heroic work endowing it with coherence and force. Sondheim always insisted on giving equal credit to his book writers, those who fed him and goaded him. It’s fitting that his last collaborator finished the epitaph.”

criticReviews.author: Peter Marks
criticReviews.excerpt: “We’ve been through sharper existential crises with convergences of Sondheim characters over the years...We’re consoled in ‘Here We Are’ with one more chance to gather together with Sondheim, to hear his irreplaceable voice on a stage. The resulting evening might not be stranded at square one, but it doesn’t satisfactorily cross the finish line, either.”

criticReviews.author: Johnny Oleksinski
criticReviews.excerpt: “The novelty of attending Sondheim’s final musical and experiencing its non-stop zaniness wear off long before ‘Here We Are’ ends, and the whole thing falls apart.”

criticReviews.author: Matt Windman
criticReviews.excerpt: " 'Here We Are' probably did not merit a full-scale, sleek, starry production – but I suppose that it had to be produced posthumously anyway in tribute to Sondheim, and diehard Sondheim fans such as myself feel as if they have an obligation to check it out."

criticReviews.author: David Gordon
criticReviews.excerpt: "Once you go with the flow, you won’t care that one character is carrying a stuffed sheep through the audience, and another is dancing with a giant bear. It’s a surrealist puzzle that Sondheim and Ives clearly enjoyed trying to solve — and we’d be hard-pressed not to enjoy it ourselves."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: “You didn't think Stephen Sondheim would say goodbye with a warm hug, did you? For his final act, our greatest musical theatre artist teamed up with playwright David Ives and director Joe Mantello on a wicked little absurdist joke designed to induce a case of the ontological heebie-jeebies...there's something extraordinarily moving about [him] in his final days tackling stylistically complex material and wondering what exactly constitutes a well-lived life. Even in his nineties, he still had plenty of questions to ask, and they're the sort that linger in the mind, sometimes uncomfortably.”

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s hard to imagine any staging more perfect than Mantello’s, whose masterful comic blocking includes a final image that’s somehow both haunting and exhilarating. Sondheim didn’t live long enough to see it, but he certainly would have heartily approved if he had.”

criticReviews.author: Michael Sommers
criticReviews.excerpt: "The potential of the story’s characters and situations seems rich enough and might well have resulted in memorable music and lyrics. Sondheim crafted some of his finest compositions in the last-minute heat of hitting production deadlines, so thoughts about what if and what could have been will haunt 'Here We Are' now and forever."

criticReviews.author: Carol Rocamora
criticReviews.excerpt: “The production values are dazzling. Joe Mantello’s smart, stylized direction of this stellar ensemble is a joy to behold...Meanwhile, for lovers of Sondheim and musical theater, it is imperative to see this vibrant production of ‘Here We Are’ at The Shed, filled with vitality and creativity.”

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: Sondheim’s music has a thrillingly familiar sound...but on first listen it seems so seamlessly integrated into Ives’ dialogue that it’s hard to imagine being turned into discrete songs for the bourgeoisie at piano bars… Ives’ adaptation streamlines Buñuel’s films for the stage and adds its own comic flourishes, but it’s faithful enough to the filmmaker’s opaque, random strangeness that some theatergoers will surely find it a challenge to interpret…

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: “...’Here We Are,’ now having its world premiere at The Shed, watching an inventive, ambitious, brilliantly acted musical without a full score by the master – and with almost every note confined to the mostly jaunty act.”

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: Sondheim’s most impactful characters stem from being misunderstood by the world, misrepresented as uglier than they really are, simpler than they really are, or confused about their priorities. This was a show that fully grasped these concepts. Though set in the future, many moments vividly evoked the present and the past. I fully support the decision to not include as much music in the second act. We all felt trapped in a room coming to terms with the last time a Sondheim show would be new.

criticReviews.author: David Sheward
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Here We Are’ is something different from all that come before it...It contains fewer songs than you would expect in a two-and-a-half hour show, but we should take what gems we can get. And somehow, the shift in perspectives from the melodic first act to the song-starved second works in its favor.”

criticReviews.author: Caroline Cao
criticReviews.excerpt: “This is a show about a bourgeoisie bubble that — for now — can afford distractions and sweep aside the questions some other time...Although ‘Here We Are’ leaves you hungry for completion, it's a slow-crawling nightmare that plink-pla-plink in your consciousness long after you leave the theatre.”

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: CRITIC’S PICK "In ‘Heroes of the Fourth Turning,’ a Red-State Unicorn: An astonishing new play by Will Arbery risks a rare stage subject: Christian conservatism."

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: 5 Stars "Danya Taymor presides over a perfect production that left me with my heart in my mouth and my pen scrambling across the page. (This is the kind of play you know you'll need to read again someday.)"

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "Deep in Red America (But Not at the Diner) in 'Heroes of the Fourth Turning'"

criticReviews.author: Vinson Cunningham
criticReviews.excerpt:
"A Play About the Nuances of Conservatism in the Trump Era
A group of friends grapple with ideologies in Will Arbery’s 'Heroes of the Fourth Turning,' at Playwrights Horizons."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "'Heroes of the Fourth Turning' and the Conservative Millennials Preparing for War"

criticReviews.author: Michael Dale
criticReviews.excerpt: "Trump-Hating Conservatives Debate Right Wing Strategies in Will Arbery's 'HEROES OF THE FOURTH TURNING.'"

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "That the playwright makes this garrulous, opinionated crew so engaging -- and their concerns so relevant -- is a mark of his considerable imagination and empathy. This new offering at Playwrights Horizons has its awkward moments, but it brings us into fresh and unfamiliar dramatic territory."

criticReviews.author: Marc Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: "A step toward increasing the dialogue — oh, so that's what that side thinks, and why they think it. Thank you, Mr. Arbery. And playwrights of the right, if you're out there, let this be an incentive: With characters and arguments this compelling, you may actually get produced."

criticReviews.author: Michael Sommers
criticReviews.excerpt: 4/5 Stars "'Millennials Argue About Our Civil Wars': Younger conservatives drunkenly debate fundamental issues at Playwrights Horizons"

criticReviews.author: Deirdre Donovan
criticReviews.excerpt: "Will Arbery's world premiere at Playwrights Horizons is an ultra-conservative reverie about our present cultural moment stirs up a perfect storm of heroesof4thturning1debate on those hot-button issues tethered to religion, politics, and the family."

criticReviews.author: Keith Paul Medelis
criticReviews.excerpt: A Theasy Best Bet "It may well be hard to watch, which is precisely why you should see it… directed with surgical precision…the set provides an emptiness that could be boring but is instead full of mystery… Do we want to root for these people? Well, sometimes. And that's the crazy part."

criticReviews.author: Brian Scott Lipton
criticReviews.excerpt: "As Arberry reveals...each one of these people is struggling, internally and/or externally in some way and it's a testament to his sharp writing and the uniformly fine cast that we do feel empathy for their plights, even if we don't particularly like them as people."

criticReviews.author: Steven Ross
criticReviews.excerpt: "It's a quick blast into a brutal beginning that shapes our perspective on these folks...we are given the difficult opportunity to join a few of them for a late night gathering to listen in as they discuss the religious war that is coming, and to try to understand the expanse of the grateful acre under their feet. It's jaw-dropping-ly difficult and ear crushingly obscure, but it works, leading us to the roots of a Christian republic and mindset that truly believes in the 'natural good'."

criticReviews.author: David Roberts
criticReviews.excerpt: "Under Danya Taymor's intuitive and exacting direction, the accomplished cast delivers believable and authentic performances and embodies the characteristics of Yeats' rough beast with cathartic effect."

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "allows us to eavesdrop on what feel like astute and authentic conversations…Terrifically acted and intellectually stimulating, 'Heroes' is also eerie, at times confusing, too long and too dark. I mean dark literally; it takes place during nighttime in a dimly lit backyard."

criticReviews.author: Samuel L. Leiter
criticReviews.excerpt: "‘Heroes…’ interested me, not because it’s a good play (which I question) but because—despite its intellectual diversions…—it presents enough real-world subject matter to compel at least temporary attention. It’s just too bad we have to wander in the weeds before getting to the good stuff."

criticReviews.author: Julia Rank
criticReviews.excerpt: "Crudup brings gravitas and quiet dignity to the role...The production looks handsome with its slatted wooden set design and Sunday-best costuming by Tim Hately."

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s entertaining and well executed but frankly bonkers...It’s just another bizarre facet of this beguilingly odd enterprise."

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "For all its early stiffness, it builds in momentum and there are moving moments. Ultimately, the political message speaks loudest, harnessing the McCarthyist fear of then and the Trumpian terror of today."

criticReviews.author: Andrzej Lukowski
criticReviews.excerpt: “High Noon the film is an all time classic. High Noon the play is an entertaining curio.”

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "Not a total misfire, then, but it doesn’t hit the mark – better to re-watch the film."

criticReviews.author: Clive Davis
criticReviews.excerpt: "Crudup proves there’s more than one way to be a hero...In the end, though, Roth doesn’t quite persuade you that this is a story that needs to be remade.”

criticReviews.author: Sarah Crompton
criticReviews.excerpt: "The rest is careful and elegantly enjoyable, but lacks that emotional punch."

criticReviews.author: Matt Wolf
criticReviews.excerpt: “But for all the elegant shifts in light and shade and haze on view before us, the play only intermittently snaps into focus: less High Noon than a middling evening.”

criticReviews.author: Alice Saville
criticReviews.excerpt: "This production tells its story carefully, but it still feels a little slow, a little crowded, a little uncertain of what it is. "

criticReviews.author: Sam Marlowe
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s still woefully little tension to engage here...As the hands on that clock finally approach 12, what you’re chiefly left thinking is, what a waste of talent – and what a waste of time."

criticReviews.author: Marianka Swain
criticReviews.excerpt: "this glamorous Cole Porter musical is a fizzy, fabulous summer party"

criticReviews.author: Clementine Scott
criticReviews.excerpt: "...High Society is, to a certain extent, an excuse for a series of absurd situations contrived to fit in as many Cole Porter songs as possible."

criticReviews.author: Nick Curtis
criticReviews.excerpt: "It's the women who impress in this reworked, airy Cole Porter musical set among a glamorous but feckless American elite, with Helen George very much in the lead."

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Immaculate in its song and dance, it is smoothly staged from the minute the (doomed) multitiered cake is wheeled on for the upcoming wedding in Long Island. But something is missing"

criticReviews.author: Arifa Akbar
criticReviews.excerpt: "Immaculate in its song and dance, it is smoothly staged from the minute the (doomed) multitiered cake is wheeled on for the upcoming wedding in Long Island."

criticReviews.author: Dominic Cavendish
criticReviews.excerpt: "Felicity Kendal steals the show in this delightfully frothy musical"

criticReviews.author: Neil Norman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Nothing can obscure Porter’s smart lyrics and the production’s upbeat, feel-good nature."

criticReviews.author: Ben Brantley
criticReviews.excerpt: "It is our very good fortune that Hillary is portrayed by Laurie Metcalf, an actress who does being thwarted better than anyone...Mr. Hnath’s play doesn’t presume to be an authoritative view of the woman behind the mask, or even of the mask itself. Instead — and this is what makes this play something more than a receptacle for recycled observations about its famous subjects — 'Hillary and Clinton' strips its protagonist down to her most ordinary self."

criticReviews.author: Mark Shenton
criticReviews.excerpt: "This is a bold theatrical speculation and uncovering...The performers don't actively imitate the real Clintons...So we're not invited to look at them through familiar eyes, but as theatrical characters who happen to be them...This gives the play a playful metatheatrical framing...But the play soon breaks free of those gestures to become a fiercely contested insider speculation about a modern marriage...The play is by turns provocative and poignant, smart and funny."

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Directed firmly and dryly by Joe Mantello, 'Hillary and Clinton' is cogent, snappy and perceptive about political and emotional realities. Much of the ground it covers might seem old to those who follow the news, but the play has now, as it could not have had in 2016, a looming sense of tragedy. Its final line, a shiv to the gut, sends you out hurting into the universe, outside the theater, where we somehow find ourselves now."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "A not particularly meaty exploration of the emotional life and logic behind a couple of particularly public figures...As the big names of the play’s title, Metcalf and John Lithgow are the very watchable wind beneath its wings — but those wings are pretty rickety...'Hillary and Clinton' isn’t really much of a comedy. It’s not much of a drama either. It’s four good actors giving bodies to a series of ideas that are, even if valid, pretty well chewed-over."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "No matter how you feel about the Clintons you’ll likely find it a once-over-lightly disappointment...As promising as this sounds on paper, it doesn’t work in the theater, in part because John Lithgow is playing Bill Clinton...Ms. Metcalf’s performance, by contrast, is nothing like an imitation, but it’s still believable in its own chilly, hard-surfaced way. What is at no time believable is the dialogue."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "Lucas Hnath’s 'Hillary and Clinton' boasts the gladdening sight of Laurie Metcalf, her every bit the equal John Lithgow and director Joe Mantello’s unfailing grace, but for all of that, no small part of the satisfaction this play delivers is recognition of an entirely different sort...The play isn’t without flaws – story-wise, it can feel a bit on the thin side...The cast, needless to say, couldn’t be better."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "If anyone could play Hillary Clinton, it’s Laurie Metcalf – and here she is giving a performance that feels painfully honest and true...The only thing wrong in this fictionalized visit to the 2008 primary is that playwright Hnath has brought nothing of substance to the table...Besides pulling off terrific political pep talks, Hnath also gets the intimate cadences of a close couple’s domestic rhythms, and lets Metcalf and Lithgow have their fun. But what about us? Where’s our fun?"

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "There's no shortage of scintillating elements in 'Hillary and Clinton'...Despite all those considerable pluses, however, Hnath's play is so slight that once its densely packed, yet nonetheless skeletal, 80 minutes are over you barely give it another thought...Sure, it's entertaining; Hnath is too smart a writer, and Metcalf and Lithgow too gifted as actors, not to keep us engaged. But not only does 'Hillary and Clinton' lack illuminating fresh perspective, it lacks drama."

criticReviews.author: Daz Gale
criticReviews.excerpt: "a show that is unashamedly stupid but incredibly intelligent in executing this stupidity"

criticReviews.author: Chris Wiegand
criticReviews.excerpt: "...frenetic fun, with the dinosaurs brought to life using physical comedy"

criticReviews.author: Oliver Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: “Alternative take on standard festive fare”

criticReviews.author: Dave Calhoun
criticReviews.excerpt: "This endearingly goofy ‘stage remake’ of Jurassic Park is an enjoyably silly"

criticReviews.author: Taylor Vaughan
criticReviews.excerpt: "...keeping us exactly between the world of the show and the world of the theatre."

criticReviews.author: Kate Soper
criticReviews.excerpt: "Hold On To Your Butts is perfect for dinosaur fans of all ages looking for a great laugh"

criticReviews.author: Daz Gale
criticReviews.excerpt: "This is a show unlike anything I have ever seen before, and I found myself as enraptured as any show I have ever seen about the rapture."

criticReviews.author: Holly O'Mahony
criticReviews.excerpt: "Impish and brimming with originality, this is fringe theatre at its most scintillating and inventive."

criticReviews.author: Miriam Sallon
criticReviews.excerpt: "Leonhard-Hooper and Brasch are, of course, fantastically talented as both writers and performers. But best of all, they're game."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "All of the performers are skilled singers and actors, filling in the generic contours of their characters with proficient professionalism...The interpolated songs are integrated into the plot smoothly enough, without lifting the show’s mild temperature...'Holiday Inn' wore out its welcome for me well before the inevitable reprise of 'White Christmas' that comes toward the close...It’s polished and pleasant. But a great gift to the theater season aborning it’s not."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Bleu has a winning muscularity and grace in various tap and ballroom sequences. Pinkham generates some chemistry with Gayer. They duet sweetly on 'White Christmas,' one of the two dozen-odd Irving Berlin ditties jukeboxed into a jazzy-elegant score. And let’s hear it for the chorus—an adorable, charmingly diverse bunch. Sure, there’s more corn and cheese served in this earnest, sweater-vested affair than any nutritionist would approve, but what harm in a cup of early eggnog?"

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "Holiday Inn' is less a 'New Irving Berlin Musical' than a new Irving Berlin medley. But that seems to have been the intention, using the cover of old-fashioned family entertainment to excuse the let’s-throw-it-all-on-the-stage aesthetic. The emphasis on brightness and speed is so extreme that the show too often feels paradoxically dim and tiresome. (The sets are flat, the lights are glare-y, and the costumes are garish.) Certainly the dialogue, which is mostly backfill, doesn’t help."

criticReviews.author: Terry Teachout
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s slick, synthetic and soulless, a musical full of robotic jokes and devoid of genuine romance. The uncharismatic leading men, Bryce Pinkham and Corbin Bleu, are to Crosby and Astaire what a Whopper is to a New York strip. The only noteworthy thing about 'Holiday Inn' is Megan Lawrence, who makes something extra-special out of the thankless part of the smart-ass second banana who doesn’t get the guy."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "An endorphin assault, inducing warm-bath pleasure like no other show since '42nd Street.' The dancing is spectacular, the singing sublime, the visuals are ingenious and, almost incidentally, there’s the cataract of Irving Berlin songs...Corbin Bleu is the discovery, tapping up a storm that recalls the young Sammy Davis Jr...Above all, Denis Jones deploys a smallish troupe of dazzling hoofers with a perfect mix of precision and abandon."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "If you’re in the mood for show that's light-on-its-feet and wall-to-wall Irving Berlin, check into Broadway’s 'Holiday Inn'...It’s familiar and vanilla-flavored fluff, but with tasty sprinkles: a fine cast, tap-happy hoofing and colorfully witty costumes."'

criticReviews.author: Frank Rizzo
criticReviews.excerpt: "Greenberg and Hodge have significantly rethought, reshaped and revitalized the script, giving the show more heart, a slightly modern sensibility and a joyful spirit. Engaging performances, dynamic dancing and a lively orchestra make it the feel-good show of the fall...The lead performers are smashing, especially Pinkham...Bleu is a spark plug of energy, and his hoofing in 'You’re Easy to Dance With' and 'Let’s Say It With Firecrackers' are two of the musical’s dance delights."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "So sweetly wholesome that you experience a sugar rush while watching it, the show is corny and predictable. But it will surely provide a happy diversion for stressed-out theatergoers during the holiday season...Pinkham and Gayer prove an appealing romantic duo, while Bleu displays his formidable singing and dancing chops in his underwritten role...There may be lulls in between, but this is a 'Holiday Inn' you'll want to check into."

criticReviews.author: Holly O'Mahony
criticReviews.excerpt: "When focused on the crux of the matter – to whom does art belong? – it's at its most compelling."

criticReviews.author: Miriam Sallon
criticReviews.excerpt: "The evening is neither offensive nor intriguing, but largely forgettable, a shame given what it might have been."

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: "the play’s dramatic method prevents its grimmer parts from being fully effective."

criticReviews.author: Amelia Merrill
criticReviews.excerpt: "Home is a fast-talking thrill of 90 minutes"

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "This play shines in the details. By the end it has won you over into joy."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: "Williams’s play is responding to trends in the heat of its moment"

criticReviews.author: Vinson Cunningham
criticReviews.excerpt: "The speech...resembles a cycle of lyric poems voiced by high-minded, plain-living folk."

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: "It may take a while for audiences to tune in to the play’s rollicking rhythms."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "...is richly poetic play about quest for inner peace"

criticReviews.author: Pete Hempstead
criticReviews.excerpt: "Under Kenny Leon’s direction, all three turn out rare tour-de-force performances"

criticReviews.author: Aliya Al-Hassan
criticReviews.excerpt: "This version feels muted; less sharp and less provocative than in 2018. This biting satire has lost its teeth."

criticReviews.author: Rosie Holmes
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘Home, I’m Darling,’ was a wonderful way to spend a few hours, showcasing wonderful performances from its stellar cast and extremely clever writing and social commentary...This is a show I highly recommend, and to be honest even without the clever writing and excellent performances, I would see it again just for the outfits.”

criticReviews.author: Ben Brantley
criticReviews.excerpt: "Wake up and smell the mai tais, New York. Las Vegas has come calling on you. And it’s on such good behavior, you’d be a churl not to embrace it...This production is a real-live, old-fashioned, deeply satisfying Broadway musical in a way few new shows are anymore. It offers the perfect sunny holiday for frozen Eastern city dwellers."

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "How to answer snobs who denounce Broadway as a cultural wasteland of gaudy lights, musical cheese and tacky titillation, a place where suckers flock to get fleeced? At least it’s not…Las Vegas? Well, the Great White Way has now become Sodom of the Southwest, and whatever happens there is definitely not staying there: Honeymoon in Vegas is too damn fun to keep secret."

criticReviews.author: Jeremy Gerard
criticReviews.excerpt: "You think they just don’t make ‘em like they used to? To find out how wrong you are, head to Broadway for a couple of hours of finger-snapping, tap-dancing, hip-swiveling, Elvis-impersonating, night-club crooning fun. That’s what the musical adaptation of Honeymoon In Vegas promises and what it delivers."

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: "There’s plenty to like about the new Broadway arrival “Honeymoon in Vegas.” That goes double for the terrific score. If only the overall production were sexier, funnier and more surprising. As is, the show is cute and old-fashioned, a good time."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "“Honeymoon In Vegas” answers gloomy Gotham’s crying need for some good old lowbrow farce. Scribe Andrew Bergman has turned his not-quite-cult 1992 movie into a not-quite-knockout Broadway musical.  But with catchy tunes and clever lyrics, sweet comic turns, and a bevy of Elvis impersonators, this brassy little show might brighten up this town over the winter."

criticReviews.author: David Rooney
criticReviews.excerpt: "It's breezy and fun, full of toe-tapping numbers, witty design touches and frequent bursts of irreverent comic inspiration. But it sputters after a tremendously entertaining first act. This is a 2½-hour musical with maybe 90 minutes' worth of decent material. Ultimately, the show feels slight."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "The sexist values of the show are not so much 1992 as 1952...This is, of course, an old-fashioned musical comedy, a genre not known for its progressive values. And the warm-centered tone is never crass or sleazy. Still, this thing badly needed the safety of some chronological remove, especially given that women buy most of the tickets to shows like this."

criticReviews.author: Elisabeth Vincentelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "The rambunctious new musical “Honeymoon in Vegas” is old-fashioned and proud of it. A big orchestra pumps out a brassy, melodic score that nods to Sinatra’s ba-da-bing days. The wacky plot could have been lifted from a 1960s caper. If only parts of the story didn’t cross the line between old-school and antediluvian."

criticReviews.author: Alexander Cohen
criticReviews.excerpt: "The serious satirical swipe at consumer culture gets sadly lost along the way, but there is plenty of humanity here to make up for it."

criticReviews.author: Dave Fargnoli
criticReviews.excerpt: “Small, significant gestures add poignant realism to even the show’s strangest, silliest moments...In an authoritarian state where profit is valued above human dignity, Fowler suggests, ordinary citizens must rely on one another for support, finding community in these small acts of kindness or defiance.”

criticReviews.author: Aleks Sierz
criticReviews.excerpt: "The overall effect is an exciting contribution to contemporary playwriting – it’s art that seems to make your mind go woo-woo."

criticReviews.author: Tom Wicker
criticReviews.excerpt: “Inventive new play ‘Hope has a Happy Meal’ at the Royal Court starts out strong...It's an opening that works by holding its nerve, building up the humour by leaving us not knowing where it’s going. The rest of the play struggles to match its effortless freewheeling wit.”

criticReviews.author: Harry Bower
criticReviews.excerpt: I would strongly recommend you buy a ticket and experience it for yourself. At the very least you will have a brilliant couple of hours of theatrical entertainment with clowns, knives, guns, beautifully raw emotional dialogue, great performances, and some exquisite nightclub dancing.”

criticReviews.author: Emma John
criticReviews.excerpt: “This is still a witty endeavour, sharply directed and joyously performed.”

criticReviews.author: Verity Healey
criticReviews.excerpt: “Despite the details of the post-democratic corporate country being too light, it’s still pleasing. It’s just that such an environment needs to have a greater impact on the life decisions made by the characters...the show is still a theatrical spectacle...And it is impossible not to be gunning for Hope – we hope that she finds what she is looking for – which is of course – herself.”

criticReviews.author: Jill Johnson
criticReviews.excerpt: Perhaps my favourite aspect of Hope has a Happy Meal is the satisfying, open-ended scene. You never know if Hope reunites with her son; the last thing the audience sees is her waiting with a happy meal, hoping. Whether it’s to analyse brilliant writing, watch some stellar actors do their thing, or hear a very extravagant yet ultimately hilarious joke, I’d highly recommend you taking a trip to the Royal Court Theatre.

criticReviews.author: Christiana Rose
criticReviews.excerpt: "A fun, fact-filled summer treat, Barmy Britain – The Best Bits! is a scream."

criticReviews.author: Chris Elwell
criticReviews.excerpt: "Exactly what it says on the tin: family theatre that hurtles through UK history in 70 minutes, packed with poo jokes to keep everyone entertained."

criticReviews.author: Anna Nichols
criticReviews.excerpt: "With great audience participation and entertainingly educational fun, Horrible Histories: Barmy Britain is the perfect summer holiday day out."

criticReviews.author: Kyle Turner
criticReviews.excerpt: "House of McQueen is mostly a house of cards."

criticReviews.author: Sara Holdren
criticReviews.excerpt: "The house might have been built for him, but Alexander McQueen is not at home."

criticReviews.author: Zachary Stewart
criticReviews.excerpt: "It gets the job done, but one wonders if a visionary like McQueen, who knew how to make his audience stew in discomfort, deserves something bolder."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "Cloud's script is an aimless, scattered series of brief episodes, leaping across time in no discernible pattern."

criticReviews.author: Frank Scheck
criticReviews.excerpt: "Unfortunately, despite the first-class production, House of McQueen never quite comes to dramatic life."

criticReviews.author: Tony Marinelli
criticReviews.excerpt: "a runway of memory, a stage-bound séance, a theatrical fashion show"

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "pieced together with bespoke extravagance.. but mostly feels like a missed opportunity"

criticReviews.author: Darryl Reilly
criticReviews.excerpt: Luke Newton is awesome as the maverick gay British fashion designer in this uneven fantasia.

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
criticReviews.excerpt: Darrah Cloud’s fever dream of a script, which is made up short scenes that jump around in time and place, is a crazy quilt of incomprehensibility that seems to lift its limited plot points from Wikipedia.

criticReviews.author: Mark Rifkin
criticReviews.excerpt: Attempts to capture the fierce energy of a McQueen runway extravaganza but instead gets mired in overuse of technology, a narrative that offers little sense of time and place, and characters that don’t grow or develop.

criticReviews.author: Mason Pilevsky
criticReviews.excerpt: A man’s life without his life’s work.

criticReviews.author: Cary Wong
criticReviews.excerpt: "Occasional flashes of cheeky fun, mostly provided by the talented design team."

criticReviews.author: Adrienne Onofri
criticReviews.excerpt: It illuminates McQueen’s chaotic personal life better than it does his iconoclastic work.

criticReviews.author: Maya Phillips
criticReviews.excerpt: "Vogel’s script creates its own piercing language for assault, harassment and all the ways our society reinforces regressive ideas about gender, sex and consent. The play is structured as an intimate collection of memories roughly organized around a set of rules about the basics of driving, as if someone had sneaked in a series of watercolor portraits between the pages of a driver’s manual. So the warnings about idling and using the reverse gear, which function as clever subtitles announcing the scenes, become subtly tied to the ways Li’l Bit fits those years of assault into her memory."

criticReviews.author: Juan Michael Porter II
criticReviews.excerpt: "How does one stage a traumatizing play that focuses on grooming, pedophilia, misogyny, and incest? In the case of Paula Vogel's Pulitzer Prize-winning play 'How I Learned to Drive,' which just premiered on Broadway at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, Mark Brokaw has opted to direct the most painful moments with a 'folks say the wackiest things' shrug. "

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: "Most good theater lives on, if it’s lucky, only in the memory of those who saw it. Manhattan Theatre Club’s revival of Paula Vogel’s 'How I Learned to Drive,' one of the signal plays of the 1990s, represents an exception. With a firm eye on the rearview mirror, this production reunites director Mark Brokaw, who helmed the show’s premiere at the Vineyard in 1997, with its two exceptional original stars, Mary-Louise Parker and David Morse"

criticReviews.author: Helen Shaw
criticReviews.excerpt: "Twenty-five years ago, Mary-Louise Parker played Li’l Bit, David Morse played Uncle Peck, and Mark Brokaw directed. Now all three are back for Broadway. Strange things happen when nostalgia gets wrapped up in the production, which is itself a cautionary tale about letting atmosphere (the night, the heat, the past) drug the senses. 'Drive' moves backward in time, revisiting earlier and earlier encounters: What we can just bear to look at when Li’l Bit is 17 gets more awful as she becomes 15, then 13, then 11."

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: "'How I Learned To Drive,' opening tonight in a first-rate Manhattan Theatre Club production at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, stars Parker as a woman looking back on, and struggling to make sense of, her relationship with her abusive Uncle Peck (Morse)."

criticReviews.author: Chris Jones
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s an unsettling experience, of course, now produced at an unsettling moment when most of our attention has been placed elsewhere. As such, it dislocates and worries in a way that I don’t think was true in 1997. You deserve to be appraised of that. As we all know, the world only spins forward and yet the habits and predilections of some always seem to find a way to adapt."

criticReviews.author: Marilyn Stasio
criticReviews.excerpt: "Vogel is a genuine wordsmith, and her language here is almost indecently seductive. A list of hard liquor drinks — luscious Pink Ladies, sloe gin fizzes, daiquiris — has the same lilting cadences as a description of a warm summer night under the stars. "

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: "Yes, the shiny, stylish model handles great on today’s theatrical highways and bumpy back roads of the Discourse. If anything, it might be too sophisticated a ride for new drivers. Why isn’t Peck’s downfall more satisfying? Why don’t we see Li’l Bit happy and successful later in life? Why does empowerment feel so melancholy? We can ask these questions all day; Paula Vogel will still be up front, eyes smiling in the rearview mirror."

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: "...is a play at odds with itself. "

criticReviews.author: Michael Sommers
criticReviews.excerpt: "...playwright infuses his comfortably familiar story with magical realism"

criticReviews.author: Scotty Bennett
criticReviews.excerpt: "a compelling story of love found, lost, and found again"

criticReviews.author: Loren Noveck
criticReviews.excerpt: "It’s a love story with an achingly, sometimes painfully slow burn"

criticReviews.author: Jonathan Mandell
criticReviews.excerpt: "lyrical and surreal"

criticReviews.author: Jesse Green
criticReviews.excerpt: “it is a welcome change that the seven autistic characters in ‘How to Dance in Ohio’ are presented, without condescension, as young adults a lot like most others, albeit with unusual gifts and challenges. That they are also played by autistic performers makes the feel-good show, which opened on Sunday at the Belasco Theater, more than a first: It’s a milestone.”

criticReviews.author: Joe Dziemianowicz
criticReviews.excerpt: “At the heart of the wonderfully performed but uneven musical ‘How to Dance in Ohio’ beats a reality for its key characters that is at once simple and profound...in the end, this worthwhile musical finds the steps to an upbeat last dance.”

criticReviews.author: Adam Feldman
criticReviews.excerpt: “All of the actors playing autistic people publicly identify as autistic themselves; they’re also all making their Broadway debuts, and while some are more experienced than others—Pearce, with his expansively emotional voice, is a ringer—they all make winsome impressions.”

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “It’s a credit to ‘How to Dance in Ohio’s’ cast that they deliver compelling performances, even when their material gets rote and didactic...If we’re here to meet these characters who aren’t going to be stand-ins for generalized traits, let’s really spend the time to get to know them all.”

criticReviews.author: Charles Isherwood
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘How to Dance in Ohio’ is certainly less raw and dispassionately observed than the movie. But this is not a documentary but a Broadway musical comedy, and as such engineered to meet the requirements of most popular entries in the genre today: uplift, sweetness, rainbow endings for all.”

criticReviews.author: Greg Evans
criticReviews.excerpt: “One of the things ‘How To Dance In Ohio’ gets so splendidly right is the easy comfort with diversity these young people with autism are graced, as if they’ve long ago made peace with the very concept of outsiderdom.”

criticReviews.author: Frank Rizzo
criticReviews.excerpt: “Under director Sammi Cannold’s staging, the actors perform with verve, commitment and authenticity — and, in a few cases, show some real star power.”

criticReviews.author: David Cote
criticReviews.excerpt: “Generically staged by Sammi Cannold, ‘How to Dance in Ohio’ was clearly made with love and will touch some hearts—on the spectrum or not—but feels synthetic and patchy when not outright tacky.”

criticReviews.author: Maya Phillips
criticReviews.excerpt: “For as much as the play aims to engage the audience in a fly-on-the-wall view of a group of people...it still neglects to provide the necessary context to make the pre-existing relationships and the character arcs feel real.”

criticReviews.author: Gillian Russo
criticReviews.excerpt: “Liliana Padilla's ‘How to Defend Yourself’ has its moments of strength...The scene is meticulously choreographed, but it doesn't feel like a polished performance. They're tapping into something bigger.”

criticReviews.author: Raven Snook
criticReviews.excerpt: "4/5 Stars! While the play has hackneyed moments, many of the interactions feel real and raw, vibrating with authenticity and considerable humor. Padilla doesn't peddle a simplified #MeToo, #AllMen message. 'How to Defend Yourself' is a tumultuous and surprisingly entertaining investigation of how all of us are warped by rape culture."

criticReviews.author: Jackson McHenry
criticReviews.excerpt: “Liliana Padilla’s ‘How to Defend Yourself’ is a hilarious and unsettling play about exercises...everyone approaches the exercises in ‘How to Defend Yourself’ with different levels of seriousness, keeping their actual intentions to themselves or not even understanding their own intentions, which makes for rich material.”

criticReviews.author: Hayley Levitt
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘How to Defend Yourself,’ directed beautifully in its New York premiere by Tony winner Rachel Chavkin, is surprisingly hilarious considering its dark subject matter.”

criticReviews.author: David Barbour
criticReviews.excerpt: Padilla's focus is extremely narrow -- if their characters have any outside interests, we don't hear about them and, aside from an ill-timed girl-on-girl kiss, they are totally heterosexual -- and yet it feels blisteringly honest, a frank portrayal nevertheless informed by a certain tenderness. Especially remarkable is the playwright's ability to foreground the comedy of calamitous social interactions without ever losing sight of the crime that has stained everyone's lives. It's an exquisite balancing act and they rarely, if ever, put a foot wrong.

criticReviews.author: Marc Miller
criticReviews.excerpt: “ ‘How to Defend Yourself’ is messy and sometimes feels less like a drama than a polemic, but people are going to be talking about it, and maybe that talk will wise some of them up.”

criticReviews.author: David Finkle
criticReviews.excerpt: “If you’ve already guessed this is an exercise in 21st century women’s empowerment, you’re on the right track.”

criticReviews.author: Tulis McCall
criticReviews.excerpt: “What a confusing production. From start to finish. The cast gives 100% and the writer could not have asked for a more committed group of performers. But even the highest of commitments has a hard time when the plot is floating around like a lost dandelion puff. The story zigs and zags and never lands.”

criticReviews.author: Thom Geier
